lessons.key_concepts: Synthesis; controlling claim across types; balance.
lessons.key_vocabulary: synthesise, balance, controlling claim, integrate, weave
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students cite the novel for emotion and the nonfiction for facts and never blend them.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a piece in the spirit of a NYT Magazine essay on a real issue.

lessons.lesson_title: Develop counterclaim and rebuttal in synthesis
lessons.learning_objective: I can develop a counterclaim and rebuttal in a synthesis essay.
lessons.key_concepts: Counterclaim placement; concession; pivot.
lessons.key_vocabulary: counterclaim, rebuttal, concession, pivot, placement
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students paste a counterclaim into the conclusion only.
lessons.real_world_hook: Engaging the strongest objection from a published response to an op-ed.

lessons.lesson_title: Use appositives and modifying clauses
lessons.learning_objective: I can add appositives and restrictive or nonrestrictive clauses to a sentence to convey precise meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Appositive structure; restrictive vs nonrestrictive.
lessons.key_vocabulary: appositive, restrictive, nonrestrictive, modify, precise
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students put commas around all relative clauses.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a wire-service news lead for clarity.

lessons.lesson_title: Apply knowledge of style for clarity
lessons.learning_objective: I can apply knowledge of language to make effective choices for meaning, style, or clarity.
lessons.key_concepts: Style for clarity; concision; precise word choice.
lessons.key_vocabulary: style, clarity, concise, precise, choice
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students confuse stylistic precision with verbosity.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a long Substack draft to half its length without losing meaning.

lessons.lesson_title: Participate in a structured academic seminar
lessons.learning_objective: I can come to a seminar prepared with evidence and follow up on peer reasoning.
lessons.key_concepts: Seminar preparation; follow-up; reasoning chains.
lessons.key_vocabulary: prepare, follow up, chain, evidence, reasoning
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students prepare to talk rather than to listen and build.
lessons.real_world_hook: Running a seminar like an editorial board meeting at a student paper.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze figurative meaning across translated poetry
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse figurative meaning and cumulative impact of word choice in translated poetry.
lessons.key_concepts: Translation choices; figurative meaning; tonal cumulative effect.
lessons.key_vocabulary: translation, figurative, cumulative, tone, choice
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume translation is neutral and ignore translator choices.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing two translations of a Neruda poem found online.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze a subject in two artistic mediums
lessons.learning_objective: I can compare a poem and a song that treat the same subject and analyse the medium effects.
lessons.key_concepts: Cross-medium analysis; image vs sound; production choices.
lessons.key_vocabulary: medium, production, image, sound, effect
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compare lyrics and poetry by genre preference, not by craft.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing a poem by Soyinka with a song on the same theme.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze structure of an essay
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how the structure of a creative nonfiction essay develops its ideas.
lessons.key_concepts: Essay structure; lyric essay; through-line.
lessons.key_vocabulary: essay structure, through-line, lyric, refrain, segment
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students expect a five-paragraph structure and find it broken.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a James Baldwin essay and naming its through-line.

lessons.lesson_title: Write a comparative analysis
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a comparative analysis of two poems or a poem and an essay.
lessons.key_concepts: Comparative analysis; balance; structure.
lessons.prerequisites: Writing literary analysis on one text.
lessons.key_vocabulary: comparative, balance, weave, axis, integrate
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write two summaries side by side and call it comparison.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a side-by-side essay for a literary magazine.

lessons.lesson_title: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language
lessons.learning_objective: I can interpret a figure of speech in context and analyse nuances in word meanings.
lessons.key_concepts: Figures of speech in context; connotation; nuance.
lessons.key_vocabulary: nuance, connotation, figure of speech, context, meaning
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students explain figurative language by restating it literally.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading Genius annotations critically and adding their own.

lessons.lesson_title: Acquire and use grade-appropriate academic words
lessons.learning_objective: I can use grade-appropriate academic words accurately in an essay.
lessons.key_concepts: Tier 2 vocabulary in context; precise usage.
lessons.key_vocabulary: Tier 2, academic, accurate, context, precise
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use big words in the wrong slot to sound smart.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a column draft so academic verbs replace vague ones.

lessons.lesson_title: Use digital media strategically in a presentation
lessons.learning_objective: I can use digital media strategically to enhance findings and reasoning in a presentation.
lessons.key_concepts: Strategic media; b-roll; data visuals.
lessons.key_vocabulary: strategic, b-roll, data, visual, enhance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students add stock photos that decorate rather than support.
lessons.real_world_hook: Designing slides like a Vox Pop short video supports its narration.

lessons.lesson_title: Reflect on growth as a reader and writer
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a one-page end-of-year reflection citing specific moments of growth.
lessons.key_concepts: Routine writing; reflection; evidence of growth.
lessons.key_vocabulary: growth, evidence, reflection, portfolio, voice
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students claim growth without showing concrete pieces of evidence.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a year-end note like a writer's annual newsletter to readers.

lessons.lesson_title: Cite evidence including uncertainty
lessons.learning_objective: I can cite strong evidence including determining where a text leaves matters uncertain.
lessons.key_concepts: Strong evidence; uncertainty; ambiguity.
lessons.key_vocabulary: uncertain, ambiguous, strong, infer, evidence
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students fill in gaps with assumptions rather than naming uncertainty.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a Puritan diary entry and naming what it leaves unsaid.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze two or more themes
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine two or more themes in a Colonial text and analyse their interaction.
lessons.key_concepts: Multiple themes; interaction; objective summary.
lessons.key_vocabulary: interact, theme, summary, intersect, develop
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students name two themes that are really the same.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a Bradstreet poem and naming two intersecting themes.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze authors' rhetoric in seminal U.S. documents
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse rhetorical features and themes of seventeenth-, eighteenth-, or nineteenth-century U.S. documents.
lessons.key_concepts: Seminal documents; rhetorical features; purpose.
lessons.key_vocabulary: seminal, document, rhetorical feature, purpose, audience
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat foundational documents only as artefacts and ignore craft.
lessons.real_world_hook: Annotating the Declaration of Independence for parallel structure.

lessons.lesson_title: Evaluate reasoning in seminal texts
lessons.learning_objective: I can evaluate reasoning in a seminal U.S. text including the application of constitutional principles.
lessons.key_concepts: Legal reasoning basics; principles in argument.
lessons.key_vocabulary: constitutional, principle, legal reasoning, evaluate, premise
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students judge reasoning by whether the conclusion matches their values.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a SCOTUS dissent excerpt and naming its reasoning steps.

lessons.lesson_title: Write argument with valid reasoning
lessons.learning_objective: I can write an argument essay with valid reasoning and relevant, sufficient evidence.
lessons.key_concepts: Reasoning chain; relevance; sufficiency.
lessons.key_vocabulary: valid, sufficient, relevant, reasoning, claim
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students offer one example as if it proves a general claim.
lessons.real_world_hook: Pitching a column on early American identity for a school history magazine.

lessons.lesson_title: Resolve complex or contested usage
lessons.learning_objective: I can resolve a contested usage issue using a style guide.
lessons.key_concepts: Style guides as authority; contested vs settled usage.
lessons.key_vocabulary: contested, style guide, usage, authority, resolve
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students argue from feel without consulting a style guide.
lessons.real_world_hook: Settling a Slack debate about whether to write data is or data are.

lessons.lesson_title: Initiate discussion on foundational texts
lessons.learning_objective: I can initiate and probe discussion on a foundational text with text-based questions.
lessons.key_concepts: Probing questions; building chains of reasoning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: probe, initiate, chain, foundational, text-based
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students ask broad opinion questions instead of text-anchored ones.
lessons.real_world_hook: Hosting a class discussion in the style of a Philosophize This episode.

lessons.lesson_title: Apply academic vocabulary at CCR level
lessons.learning_objective: I can use academic vocabulary precisely in an analytic essay on a Colonial text.
lessons.key_concepts: Tier 2 vocabulary at CCR level; precision over inflation.
lessons.key_vocabulary: precise, inflate, accurate, register, CCR
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use Latinate verbs whose meaning they do not quite know.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a draft for precise academic verbs the way a research editor would.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze impact of author's choices on a story
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse the impact of an author's choices about elements of a Romantic novel.
lessons.key_concepts: Author choices; effect on theme; coherence of devices.
lessons.key_vocabulary: choice, effect, coherence, develop, structure
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students confuse plot summary with analysis of authorial choice.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing Hawthorne's symbol choices the way a literary podcast unpacks decisions.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze figurative and connotative meaning
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse the impact of figurative and connotative meanings on tone in a Romantic poem.
lessons.key_concepts: Figurative; connotation; tone; cumulative.
lessons.key_vocabulary: connotation, figurative, tone, cumulative, choice
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students label devices without showing impact on tone.
lessons.real_world_hook: Annotating an Emerson essay for connotative weight.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze structure choices contributing to meaning
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how the structure of specific parts of a Romantic novel contributes to overall meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Local structure; chapter design; sequencing.
lessons.key_vocabulary: structure, chapter, sequencing, design, contribute
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students consider only overall plot structure, not local design.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing chapter design the way a writer's room plans an episode arc.

lessons.lesson_title: Demonstrate knowledge of foundational American works
lessons.learning_objective: I can compare two foundational American texts on a shared theme.
lessons.key_concepts: Foundational works; comparative analysis; theme.
lessons.key_vocabulary: foundational, treat, theme, contrast, period
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compare biographies of authors instead of the texts themselves.
lessons.real_world_hook: Pairing Emerson's Self-Reliance with a current self-help podcast for contrast.

lessons.lesson_title: Write literary analysis on symbol and theme
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a literary analysis on symbol and theme in The Scarlet Letter.
lessons.key_concepts: Symbol analysis; theme integration; controlling claim.
lessons.key_vocabulary: symbol, theme, integrate, claim, develop
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students list symbols and stop without showing meaning.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a piece pitched to an undergraduate literature journal.

lessons.lesson_title: Use varied syntax for effect
lessons.learning_objective: I can vary syntax for effect, including cumulative, periodic, and balanced sentences.
lessons.key_concepts: Sentence types as rhetorical choices.
lessons.key_vocabulary: cumulative, periodic, balanced, syntax, effect
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students default to short subject-verb-object sentences in all analysis.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a TED-style talk for varied sentence rhythm.

lessons.lesson_title: Evaluate effectiveness of a text's structure
lessons.learning_objective: I can evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses to make a point clear and convincing.
lessons.key_concepts: Structure as choice; effectiveness; counterfactual structures.
lessons.key_vocabulary: structure, effective, counterfactual, clear, convincing
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rate structure by whether they personally enjoyed reading.
lessons.real_world_hook: Auditing a podcast script for structural effectiveness.

lessons.lesson_title: Synthesise multiple sources for argument
lessons.learning_objective: I can synthesise multiple sources on a topic to support an argument.
lessons.key_concepts: Synthesis; source integration; controlling claim.
lessons.key_vocabulary: synthesise, integrate, controlling, weave, balance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students stack sources without integrating them.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a feature like a New Yorker Talk of the Town item.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze point of view including irony
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse a case in which point of view requires distinguishing what is directly stated from what is meant.
lessons.key_concepts: Verbal irony; satire; understatement.
lessons.key_vocabulary: satire, irony, understatement, sarcasm, voice
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students take ironic statements at face value.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a chapter of Huck Finn and a satirical newsletter for layered voice.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze a complex set of ideas in informational text
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse a complex set of ideas in a piece of literary nonfiction.
lessons.key_concepts: Complex argument; interaction of ideas.
lessons.key_vocabulary: complex, interaction, layered, develop, integrate
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students simplify a layered argument into a single thesis.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a James Baldwin essay and mapping its layered claims.

lessons.lesson_title: Determine refined meaning of a key term
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine how the meaning of a key term is refined over the course of a text.
lessons.key_concepts: Key term tracking; redefinition; semantic shift.
lessons.key_vocabulary: key term, refine, shift, redefine, track
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume a key term means the same thing throughout an essay.
lessons.real_world_hook: Tracking the word freedom across a Frederick Douglass speech.

lessons.lesson_title: Determine effective rhetoric in nonfiction
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine an author's point of view in which the rhetoric is particularly effective.
lessons.key_concepts: Effective rhetoric; stance; ethos through diction.
lessons.key_vocabulary: stance, rhetoric, effective, ethos, diction
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students declare rhetoric effective because they agreed with the conclusion.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing two op-eds on the same topic for effective rhetoric.

lessons.lesson_title: Write argument bridging literature and current issue
lessons.learning_objective: I can write an argument essay using literature to support a position on a current issue.
lessons.key_concepts: Bridge essay; controlling claim; counterclaim.
lessons.key_vocabulary: bridge, current, link, controlling, counterclaim
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students argue about the text only or about the issue only.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing an essay that could appear in a school's social issues issue of the magazine.

lessons.lesson_title: Evaluate speaker's evidence and rhetoric
lessons.learning_objective: I can evaluate a speaker's reasoning, evidence, and rhetoric in a recorded address.
lessons.key_concepts: Spoken evaluation; bias detection; structure.
lessons.key_vocabulary: evaluate, bias, structure, rhetoric, address
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rate addresses by personal style alone.
lessons.real_world_hook: Annotating a current congressional hearing clip for reasoning and rhetoric.

lessons.lesson_title: Use signal phrases for source integration
lessons.learning_objective: I can integrate sources using signal phrases that include credentials, stance, and context.
lessons.key_concepts: Signal phrase craft; ethical attribution.
lessons.key_vocabulary: signal phrase, credential, stance, context, attribute
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students drop quotes with author tags only and no context.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a longform article so each source feels properly introduced.

lessons.lesson_title: Conduct a structured academic seminar
lessons.learning_objective: I can lead a structured academic seminar with text-based evidence and follow up on peer claims.
lessons.key_concepts: Seminar leadership; chain of reasoning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: lead, structured, evidence, chain, follow up
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students dominate when leading and stop building chains of reasoning.
lessons.real_world_hook: Leading a seminar in the style of a public radio panel show.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze how an author's choices develop characters
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how an author's choices develop and relate elements of a modern American novel.
lessons.key_concepts: Modernist choices; character relations; theme.
lessons.key_vocabulary: modernist, relate, choice, develop, theme
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students analyse characters in isolation rather than their relations.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing relationships in a Toni Morrison chapter.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze multiple interpretations of a text
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse multiple interpretations of a story, drama, or poem.
lessons.key_concepts: Multiple interpretations; performance and reading; production.
lessons.key_vocabulary: interpretation, multiple, performance, production, valid
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students declare one interpretation correct without analysis.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing two staged versions of a contemporary play streamed online.

lessons.lesson_title: Integrate multiple sources of information across media
lessons.learning_objective: I can integrate multiple sources of information in different media to address a question.
lessons.key_concepts: Cross-media integration; source synthesis.
lessons.key_vocabulary: integrate, media, address, source, synthesise
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students summarise each source separately and never bring them together.
lessons.real_world_hook: Researching a topic with text, audio, data, and image sources.

lessons.lesson_title: Conduct sustained research and synthesise
lessons.learning_objective: I can conduct a sustained research project that synthesises multiple sources on a subject.
lessons.key_concepts: Sustained research; depth; synthesis.
lessons.key_vocabulary: sustained, depth, synthesise, focus, iterate
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat sustained research as longer short research.
lessons.real_world_hook: Producing research like a midlength feature for a magazine.

lessons.lesson_title: Write a research paper with controlling idea
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a research paper with a strong controlling idea and disciplined source use.
lessons.key_concepts: Controlling idea; discipline of evidence; cohesion.
lessons.key_vocabulary: controlling, discipline, cohesion, develop, support
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students paste source content with no controlling idea.
lessons.real_world_hook: Submitting a piece like a feature for a college-style student paper.

lessons.lesson_title: Write a college admissions essay
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a personal essay of about 650 words that meets a Common App style prompt.
lessons.key_concepts: College essay structure; voice; reflection.
lessons.key_vocabulary: personal, voice, prompt, reflect, concise
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students try to sound impressive instead of specific.
lessons.real_world_hook: Drafting a Common App-style essay for a real prompt.

lessons.lesson_title: Demonstrate command of conventions
lessons.learning_objective: I can demonstrate command of conventions of capitalisation, punctuation, and spelling for academic writing.
lessons.key_concepts: Editing for conventions; hyphenation; spelling.
lessons.key_vocabulary: convention, capitalisation, hyphenation, spell, edit
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rely on autocorrect for hyphenation rules.
lessons.real_world_hook: Submitting copy as a student journalist would for a final issue.

lessons.lesson_title: Present research with strategic media
lessons.learning_objective: I can present research with strategic digital media that supports findings and reasoning.
lessons.key_concepts: Strategic media; data viz; reasoning support.
lessons.key_vocabulary: strategic, data viz, support, reasoning, findings
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students put their entire paper on slides and read it.
lessons.real_world_hook: Presenting like a podcaster doing a live event.

lessons.lesson_title: Cite evidence including uncertainty in epic poetry
lessons.learning_objective: I can cite strong evidence in an epic and name where the text leaves meaning uncertain.
lessons.key_concepts: Strong evidence in archaic verse; ambiguity.
lessons.prerequisites: Citing strong evidence in modern texts.
lessons.key_vocabulary: uncertain, archaic, kenning, ambiguous, infer
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume archaic verse is simply old, not deliberately ambiguous.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a Beowulf passage and naming what remains uncertain about Grendel.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze figurative meaning in Old and Middle English
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse figurative meaning in a passage of Beowulf or a Canterbury Tale.
lessons.key_concepts: Kennings; alliterative verse; Middle English vocabulary.
lessons.prerequisites: Analysing figurative meaning in modern poetry.
lessons.key_vocabulary: kenning, alliterative, Middle English, figurative, archaic
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students try to translate every word literally without studying its function.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing a kenning to a modern compound nickname in a podcast.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze structure of a frame narrative
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how a frame narrative shapes meaning in the Canterbury Tales.
lessons.key_concepts: Frame narrative; embedded story; structural irony.
lessons.key_vocabulary: frame, embedded, structural irony, layered, narrator
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat the General Prologue and the Tales as if they share one voice.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing Chaucer's frame to a podcast host introducing each guest.

lessons.lesson_title: Demonstrate knowledge of foundational British works
lessons.learning_objective: I can demonstrate knowledge of foundational works in the British tradition.
lessons.key_concepts: Foundational British texts; chronology; influence.
lessons.prerequisites: Demonstrating knowledge of foundational American works.
lessons.key_vocabulary: foundational, influence, chronology, British, tradition
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat all old British texts as one period.
lessons.real_world_hook: Building a class timeline of British literature for a course blog.

lessons.lesson_title: Write literary analysis on heroic code or frame
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a literary analysis essay on the heroic code or on Chaucer's frame.
lessons.key_concepts: Analytic claim about craft; integration of archaic evidence.
lessons.key_vocabulary: heroic code, frame, claim, integrate, analyse
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students summarise Beowulf or Chaucer plot rather than analysing structure.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing for a course blog modelled on the JSTOR Daily site.

lessons.lesson_title: Resolve contested usage with style guides
lessons.learning_objective: I can resolve a usage question by consulting two style guides and citing them.
lessons.key_concepts: Style guides; usage debates; authority.
lessons.key_vocabulary: style guide, usage, authority, consult, cite
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students cite a website that disagrees with multiple major style guides.
lessons.real_world_hook: Settling a question about Oxford comma usage for a publication style sheet.

lessons.lesson_title: Initiate discussion on archaic texts
lessons.learning_objective: I can initiate and lead discussion on an archaic text with text-based questions.
lessons.key_concepts: Discussion on translation; structural questions; close reading.
lessons.key_vocabulary: initiate, archaic, translation, structural, close reading
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students avoid archaic texts in discussion and stay general.
lessons.real_world_hook: Leading a discussion like a host of an audiobook companion podcast.

lessons.lesson_title: Apply diction across registers
lessons.learning_objective: I can revise a paragraph to control diction across formal and creative registers.
lessons.key_concepts: Register; diction; consistency.
lessons.key_vocabulary: register, diction, formal, creative, consistent
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students mix archaic flourish with modern slang and call it style.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a podcast script for register fit with the show's brand.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze themes interacting in a tragedy
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how two or more themes interact in a Shakespearean tragedy.
lessons.key_concepts: Theme interaction; tragic structure; thematic counterpoint.
lessons.prerequisites: Tracking single theme in long form.
lessons.key_vocabulary: interact, counterpoint, tragedy, develop, theme
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students keep themes parallel without exploring how they cut against each other.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing intersecting themes in a Best Picture-style prestige film.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze impact of choices on a play
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how an author's choices about how to develop and relate elements shape a tragedy.
lessons.key_concepts: Soliloquy, foil, structure; tragic mechanism.
lessons.key_vocabulary: soliloquy, foil, tragic, hubris, mechanism
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students attribute tragedy to fate rather than to choices in the play.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing a tragic hero's choices like a critic on a film breakdown podcast.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze metaphysical conceit
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse a metaphysical conceit in a Donne or Marvell poem.
lessons.key_concepts: Conceit; extended metaphor; argument in verse.
lessons.key_vocabulary: conceit, extended metaphor, argument, paradox, witty
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat any extended metaphor as a conceit.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing a Donne conceit to a viral analogy in a modern essay.

lessons.lesson_title: Write argument on tragic hero or conceit
lessons.learning_objective: I can write an argument essay on tragic hero or metaphysical conceit using textual evidence.
lessons.key_concepts: Argument from craft; balanced evidence; counterclaim.
lessons.key_vocabulary: tragic hero, conceit, evidence, counterclaim, claim
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students argue tragic hero status from one trait such as ambition only.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a piece like an analysis on a literary podcast's blog.

lessons.lesson_title: Use cumulative and periodic sentences
lessons.learning_objective: I can write cumulative and periodic sentences in analytic prose for effect.
lessons.key_concepts: Cumulative addition; periodic delay; rhetorical effect.
lessons.key_vocabulary: cumulative, periodic, addition, delay, effect
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students cannot tell a cumulative sentence apart from a long string of fragments.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a graduation speech draft for memorable sentence shapes.

lessons.lesson_title: Demonstrate hortative, conditional, and subjunctive moods
lessons.learning_objective: I can use hortative, conditional, and subjunctive moods for effect in formal writing.
lessons.key_concepts: Verb mood in formal prose; advanced syntax.
lessons.key_vocabulary: hortative, conditional, subjunctive, mood, formal
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students drop the subjunctive even in if-then constructions.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a model UN resolution where conditional clauses matter.

lessons.lesson_title: Participate in academic seminar on tragedy
lessons.learning_objective: I can participate in a structured seminar on tragedy with text-based questions and follow-up.
lessons.key_concepts: Seminar norms; reasoning chains; evidence ladder.
lessons.key_vocabulary: ladder, chain, follow up, anchor, evidence
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students offer opinion only and skip the anchoring quotation.
lessons.real_world_hook: Hosting a discussion like a guest on a literature podcast.

lessons.lesson_title: Take an AP-style timed essay on prose
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a 40-minute AP-style essay on a prose passage with thesis and support.
lessons.key_concepts: Timed essay; thesis on the fly; quick evidence selection.
lessons.key_vocabulary: timed, thesis, prose, AP, support
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students plan too long and never get to the third body paragraph.
lessons.real_world_hook: Drafting under timed conditions like an AP exam Q2 task.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze structure parts contributing to whole
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how structural choices in specific parts of a Romantic or Victorian novel contribute to overall meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Volume and chapter design; serial publication context.
lessons.key_vocabulary: volume, chapter, serial, design, contribute
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students forget that some Victorian novels appeared serially and were shaped by that.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing chapter design the way a season finale planner thinks about reveals.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze layered point of view including satire
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse a case where point of view requires distinguishing the stated from the meant.
lessons.key_concepts: Satire; free indirect discourse; layered voice.
lessons.key_vocabulary: satire, free indirect, layered, voice, irony
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students miss free indirect discourse and treat narration as flat.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading an Austen chapter and a satirical newsletter for layered voice.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze multiple interpretations of a novel
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse multiple interpretations of a Romantic novel and evaluate each one.
lessons.key_concepts: Adaptation; performance; critical reception.
lessons.key_vocabulary: interpretation, adaptation, performance, reception, evaluate
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rank adaptations by fidelity to plot only.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing a Frankenstein adaptation on stage to a recent film version.

lessons.lesson_title: Write comparative analysis novel plus poetry
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a comparative analysis essay using a novel and a poem from the same period.
lessons.key_concepts: Comparative axis; period context; thematic linking.
lessons.key_vocabulary: comparative, axis, period, link, integrate
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write two summaries side by side and call it comparison.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a side-by-side analysis for a literary student journal.

lessons.lesson_title: Use cohesion across sections of long writing
lessons.learning_objective: I can use cohesion devices to link sections of a long essay across pages.
lessons.key_concepts: Long-form cohesion; recurrent threads; transitions.
lessons.key_vocabulary: cohesion, thread, link, transition, sustain
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students start each section as if it were standalone.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a research paper to read as one piece, not a stack of paragraphs.

lessons.lesson_title: Interpret figures of speech in context
lessons.learning_objective: I can interpret figures of speech in context, including pathetic fallacy and synecdoche.
lessons.key_concepts: Pathetic fallacy; synecdoche; context-dependent meaning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: pathetic fallacy, synecdoche, context, interpret, figure
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students label pathetic fallacy as personification and stop.
lessons.real_world_hook: Annotating a Wordsworth poem on the Poetry Foundation site.

lessons.lesson_title: Take AP-style timed essay on poetry
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a 40-minute AP-style essay on a poem with thesis and support.
lessons.key_concepts: Timed poetry essay; quick close reading; evidence selection.
lessons.key_vocabulary: timed, poem, AP, thesis, close reading
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students paraphrase the poem instead of analysing it.
lessons.real_world_hook: Drafting under timed conditions like an AP exam Q1 task.

lessons.lesson_title: Adapt speech to varied audiences
lessons.learning_objective: I can deliver the same analysis adapted to peer, professional, and general public audiences.
lessons.key_concepts: Audience adaptation; register; example choice.
lessons.key_vocabulary: audience, adapt, register, example, scope
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students translate vocabulary only and not register or examples.
lessons.real_world_hook: Pitching the same idea on a school podcast and on a teacher's panel.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze point of view in postcolonial fiction
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how a postcolonial work draws on and transforms its sources.
lessons.key_concepts: Postcolonial response; rewriting; counter-narrative.
lessons.key_vocabulary: postcolonial, counter-narrative, rewriting, transform, source
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat a counter-narrative as just a different story.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing Achebe on Heart of Darkness as a counter-narrative discussion.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze themes interacting across two works
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how themes interact across two works from different traditions.
lessons.key_concepts: Cross-tradition themes; comparative reading.
lessons.key_vocabulary: interact, cross-tradition, theme, complex, develop
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students see themes as the same when traditions are different.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing themes in a modernist British novel and a postcolonial African novel.

lessons.lesson_title: Integrate sources across media for research
lessons.learning_objective: I can integrate multiple sources of information across media to address a research question.
lessons.key_concepts: Multi-media research; synthesis; balanced sources.
lessons.key_vocabulary: integrate, media, balanced, synthesise, question
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rely heavily on one media type for convenience.
lessons.real_world_hook: Producing a backgrounder like a major newsroom's explainer team.

lessons.lesson_title: Conduct capstone research with depth
lessons.learning_objective: I can plan and conduct a capstone research project of 3000 to 4000 words across two periods or traditions.
lessons.key_concepts: Capstone planning; iteration; controlling claim.
lessons.key_vocabulary: capstone, iterate, period, tradition, control
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students plan a question they cannot finish in the available time.
lessons.real_world_hook: Producing a capstone like an undergraduate thesis preview.

lessons.lesson_title: Synthesise sources for capstone argument
lessons.learning_objective: I can synthesise multiple authoritative sources into a coherent capstone argument.
lessons.key_concepts: Synthesis at scale; quality of evidence; integration.
lessons.key_vocabulary: synthesise, authoritative, integrate, evidence, controlling
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assemble sources and never integrate them.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing like a long-form Atlantic feature.

lessons.lesson_title: Write a college admissions essay with reflection
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a college admissions essay that reflects on a specific moment with voice and reflection.
lessons.key_concepts: Personal essay; voice; reflection at the close.
lessons.key_vocabulary: voice, reflection, moment, scene, specific
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose a worthy topic and skip the actual scene.
lessons.real_world_hook: Drafting an essay for a real Common App prompt before fall applications.

lessons.lesson_title: Edit for advanced conventions and clarity
lessons.learning_objective: I can edit a capstone draft for advanced conventions, varied syntax, and clarity.
lessons.key_concepts: Final editing pass; advanced conventions; clarity.
lessons.key_vocabulary: edit, convention, syntax, clarity, polish
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students proofread only the first and last pages of a long paper.
lessons.real_world_hook: Filing copy as a freelance writer would for final publication.

lessons.lesson_title: Defend a senior portfolio orally
lessons.learning_objective: I can present and defend a senior portfolio with three to five anchor pieces in a 10-minute exhibition.
lessons.key_concepts: Portfolio defence; reasoning chain; reflection.
lessons.key_vocabulary: defend, portfolio, exhibition, anchor, reflect
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students present polished work without explaining how it shows growth.
lessons.real_world_hook: Defending a portfolio like a senior project at a model school exhibition night.

lessons.lesson_title: Map the rhetorical situation
lessons.learning_objective: I can identify the exigence, purpose, audience, context, and message of a nonfiction text.
lessons.key_concepts: Rhetorical situation; exigence; purpose; audience; context; message; the writer as a deliberate decision-maker.
lessons.prerequisites: Identifying an author's point of view and purpose in an informational text.
lessons.key_vocabulary: rhetorical situation, exigence, purpose, audience, context, message
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat exigence as the topic itself rather than the specific event or problem that prompted the writer to speak at that moment.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a CEO's public apology after a data breach and naming exactly what forced the statement out that week.

lessons.lesson_title: Explain how choices fit the situation
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how a writer's choices respond to a specific audience, purpose, and context.
lessons.key_concepts: Choices respond to the situation; audience beliefs, values, and needs; the same message shifts for different audiences.
lessons.key_vocabulary: rhetorical choice, appeal, values, beliefs, tone, persona
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students list ethos, pathos, and logos as labels instead of explaining why a particular choice would work on this particular audience.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing how a city council member pitches the same budget to taxpayers and to a teachers' union.

lessons.lesson_title: Rhetorical appeals beyond labels
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyze how a writer builds credibility, emotion, and logic as choices rather than as a checklist.
lessons.key_concepts: Ethos, pathos, and logos as effects of concrete choices (anecdote, statistic, shared identity, concession); one choice can do several jobs.
lessons.prerequisites: Explaining how choices fit the situation.
lessons.key_vocabulary: ethos, pathos, logos, anecdote, concession, credibility
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students believe naming an appeal ("this is pathos") is analysis; AP readers reward explaining the function of the choice, not identifying it.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analyzing a public-service ad that pairs a statistic with a single family's story.

lessons.lesson_title: Write for an audience
lessons.learning_objective: I can write an introduction and conclusion that fit my audience and purpose.
lessons.key_concepts: Introductions establish exigence and stakes; conclusions extend significance; adjusting register and evidence to audience knowledge and beliefs.
lessons.prerequisites: Identifying audience and purpose in others' writing.
lessons.key_vocabulary: introduction, conclusion, register, stakes, significance, audience awareness
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students open every essay with a dictionary definition or "Since the dawn of time" instead of an exigence that fits the prompt.
lessons.real_world_hook: Rewriting a school-board email so it persuades skeptical parents rather than fellow students.

lessons.lesson_title: Identify claims and evidence
lessons.learning_objective: I can distinguish a writer's claims from the evidence offered to support them.
lessons.key_concepts: Claim versus evidence; types of evidence (data, expert testimony, anecdote, example, analogy); evaluating relevance and sufficiency.
lessons.key_vocabulary: claim, evidence, data, testimony, anecdote, sufficiency, relevance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat any sentence with a number in it as strong evidence without asking whether it actually supports the specific claim.
lessons.real_world_hook: Checking whether a viral fitness post's statistics really prove its headline.

lessons.lesson_title: Commentary: explain how evidence proves the claim
lessons.learning_objective: I can write commentary that explains how and why my evidence supports my claim.
lessons.key_concepts: Claim-evidence-commentary chain; commentary answers "so what?" and "how does this prove it?"; commentary should outweigh quotation.
lessons.key_vocabulary: commentary, warrant, explain, connect, line of reasoning, significance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students "drop" a quote and move on, or paraphrase the quote and call it commentary; Chief Reader reports name dropped quotes and summary as top Row B weaknesses.
lessons.real_world_hook: Defending a product recommendation at work by explaining why the numbers matter, not just pasting the chart.

lessons.lesson_title: Integrate evidence smoothly
lessons.learning_objective: I can embed quotations and paraphrases with signal phrases and accurate context.
lessons.key_concepts: Signal phrases; embedding partial quotations in my own syntax; paraphrase versus quotation; keeping quotes short and purposeful.
lessons.key_vocabulary: signal phrase, embed, paraphrase, ellipsis, brackets, attribution
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students paste long block quotes, assuming more quoted text means more evidence points.
lessons.real_world_hook: Quoting a source precisely in a news-style article without misrepresenting it.

lessons.lesson_title: Qualify a claim and address counterarguments
lessons.learning_objective: I can qualify a claim with modifiers, concessions, and rebuttals.
lessons.key_concepts: Qualifiers (often, in most cases); concession and rebuttal; alternative perspectives strengthen rather than weaken an argument.
lessons.prerequisites: Writing a claim with evidence and commentary.
lessons.key_vocabulary: qualify, concede, rebut, counterargument, modifier, nuance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think acknowledging the other side weakens their position, or they raise a counterargument and never answer it.
lessons.real_world_hook: Arguing for a later school start time while honestly answering the bus-schedule objection.

lessons.lesson_title: What makes a thesis defensible
lessons.learning_objective: I can tell the difference between a defensible thesis and a summary or restatement of the prompt.
lessons.key_concepts: Row A (0-1 point): thesis must take a defensible position that responds to the prompt; summary, restating the prompt, or a mere fact earns 0.
lessons.key_vocabulary: thesis, defensible, position, restate, summary, Row A
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write a thesis that only summarizes the issue ("There are pros and cons to GPS technology"); the 2025 Chief Reader Report names this as the typical reason the thesis point was missed.
lessons.real_world_hook: Telling a friend not just what a movie is about but whether it is worth seeing and why.

lessons.lesson_title: Thesis formulas for each essay type
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a thesis tailored to the synthesis, rhetorical analysis, and argument prompts.
lessons.key_concepts: Synthesis and argument theses take a position on the issue; rhetorical analysis theses name the writer's choices and connect them to purpose; previewing a line of reasoning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: position, rhetorical choice, purpose, preview, because-clause
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write rhetorical analysis theses that list devices ("uses ethos, pathos, and logos") without stating what the writer is trying to achieve; the rubric says a thesis fails if it does not address the rhetorical choices.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing a thesis for a debate brief with the thesis of a film review.

lessons.lesson_title: Revise a weak thesis
lessons.learning_objective: I can revise vague, summary, or overly broad theses into precise, arguable ones.
lessons.key_concepts: Revision moves: add a because-clause, narrow scope, replace vague verbs ("uses," "shows") with precise ones, add a qualifier.
lessons.prerequisites: Thesis formulas for each essay type.
lessons.key_vocabulary: vague, precise, scope, qualifier, specific verb, revise
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think a longer thesis is a better thesis, or believe a thesis must have exactly three prongs.
lessons.real_world_hook: Tightening a vague college-essay opening into a clear claim about yourself.

lessons.lesson_title: Thesis placement and complexity
lessons.learning_objective: I can place my thesis where readers expect it and build complexity into the claim itself.
lessons.key_concepts: Thesis may appear in intro or conclusion but must be clear; complex theses acknowledge tension or conditions (although X, Y) and set up the sophistication point.
lessons.key_vocabulary: complexity, tension, condition, although-clause, placement
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume a "both sides" thesis is automatically complex; a thesis that refuses to take a position still fails Row A.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing an op-ed headline and subhead that takes a stance but acknowledges a trade-off.

lessons.lesson_title: Trace a writer's line of reasoning
lessons.learning_objective: I can describe a writer's line of reasoning and explain how each claim supports the thesis.
lessons.key_concepts: Line of reasoning as the sequence of claims that justify the thesis; how paragraphs build on each other; gaps in reasoning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: line of reasoning, sequence, build, support, gap, unify
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think line of reasoning means the order of paragraphs rather than the logical connections between claims.
lessons.real_world_hook: Outlining the argument of a TED talk to see if each point actually leads to the conclusion.

lessons.lesson_title: Methods of development
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain and use methods of development such as comparison, cause-effect, definition, and narration.
lessons.key_concepts: Methods of development (narration, description, comparison-contrast, definition, cause-effect, problem-solution); choosing a method that fits purpose.
lessons.key_vocabulary: method of development, comparison, cause-effect, definition, narration, problem-solution
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think organization is only five-paragraph structure and ignore how a writer's chosen method advances the argument.
lessons.real_world_hook: Structuring a lab-funding proposal as problem-solution rather than as a list of features.

lessons.lesson_title: Transitions that show logic
lessons.learning_objective: I can use transitions that show the logical relationship between ideas.
lessons.key_concepts: Transitional words, phrases, and sentences; addition, contrast, cause, concession, sequence; transitions linking claims to the thesis.
lessons.key_vocabulary: transition, contrast, concession, consequently, nevertheless, cohesion
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use "Also" or "Another example is" for every paragraph, which signals a list rather than a developing argument.
lessons.real_world_hook: Smoothing a group-project slide deck so each slide clearly leads to the next.

lessons.lesson_title: Build a body paragraph that advances the argument
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a body paragraph with a topic claim, evidence, and commentary that connects back to my thesis.
lessons.key_concepts: Topic claim tied to thesis; evidence; commentary that explains and connects; concluding link to the line of reasoning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: topic sentence, claim, commentary, connect, cohesion, line of reasoning
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students start body paragraphs with a fact or quote instead of a claim, leaving the reader to guess the point.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing one tight paragraph to persuade a coach to change practice times.

lessons.lesson_title: Read the passage like a rhetorician
lessons.learning_objective: I can annotate a passage for its rhetorical situation and the writer's key choices during the reading period.
lessons.key_concepts: Q2 task: analyze how a writer's choices contribute to purpose; annotation plan (SPACE: speaker, purpose, audience, context, exigence); tracking shifts.
lessons.key_vocabulary: annotate, shift, choice, purpose, speaker, SPACE
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students annotate every device they can spot instead of the few choices that most clearly serve the purpose.
lessons.real_world_hook: Breaking down a commencement speech to see why one moment made the audience applaud.

lessons.lesson_title: Choices, not devices
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain what a writer's choice does and why it works for this audience.
lessons.key_concepts: Verb-driven analysis (the writer juxtaposes, concedes, escalates); what the choice does, how it affects the audience, why it serves the purpose.
lessons.prerequisites: Read the passage like a rhetorician.
lessons.key_vocabulary: juxtapose, escalate, concede, contrast, effect, function
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students list rhetorical devices without explaining their function, a weakness Chief Reader reports flag year after year.
lessons.real_world_hook: Explaining why a protest sign's short, repeated phrase is more powerful than a paragraph.

lessons.lesson_title: Organize chronologically or by choice
lessons.learning_objective: I can organize a rhetorical analysis essay so my commentary follows the writer's line of reasoning.
lessons.key_concepts: Chronological organization by sections of the passage versus organization by choice; tracking how strategies build across the text.
lessons.key_vocabulary: chronological, section, shift, progression, strategy
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students organize by ethos, pathos, logos paragraphs, which fragments the writer's argument and usually leads to labeling instead of analysis.
lessons.real_world_hook: Narrating how a podcast host shifts from humor to urgency over an episode.

lessons.lesson_title: Score and revise a Q2 essay
lessons.learning_objective: I can score a rhetorical analysis essay on the 6-point rubric and revise it to earn more points.
lessons.key_concepts: Rubric rows: thesis 0-1, evidence and commentary 0-4, sophistication 0-1; a 4 in Row B consistently explains how choices serve purpose; timed 40-minute practice.
lessons.key_vocabulary: Row A, Row B, Row C, holistic, revise, timed
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students believe a long essay scores higher; Row B rewards consistent explanation of choices, not length or number of devices.
lessons.real_world_hook: Scoring an anonymous sample essay the way an AP reader would in June.

lessons.lesson_title: Unpack an argument prompt
lessons.learning_objective: I can identify the precise question an argument prompt asks and take a defensible position on it.
lessons.key_concepts: Q3 task: develop a position on a concept or claim using evidence from reading, experience, or observation; identifying key terms; avoiding off-topic positions.
lessons.key_vocabulary: prompt, position, key term, defensible, scope
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students answer a related but easier question than the one asked (writing about technology in general when the prompt asks about a specific claim).
lessons.real_world_hook: Responding to a scholarship prompt that asks a narrow question, not a general one.

lessons.lesson_title: Find specific evidence from your own knowledge
lessons.learning_objective: I can brainstorm and select specific, relevant evidence from history, current events, literature, and experience.
lessons.key_concepts: Specific beats general; an evidence bank (historical events, current events, science, books, personal experience); choosing evidence that fits the claim.
lessons.key_vocabulary: specific, general, evidence bank, example, relevance, illustration
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use hypothetical or vague evidence ("many people believe") that earns low Row B scores.
lessons.real_world_hook: Building a personal evidence bank you can reuse in debates and interviews.

lessons.lesson_title: Develop reasoning with counterarguments
lessons.learning_objective: I can deepen an argument by addressing counterclaims and explaining limits of my position.
lessons.key_concepts: Concession-rebuttal paragraphs; conditions and limits; reasoning that explains why evidence matters rather than listing examples.
lessons.key_vocabulary: concession, rebuttal, limit, condition, reasoning, nuance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students stack three examples that all prove the same narrow point and never explain the reasoning behind them.
lessons.real_world_hook: Arguing about a phone ban in school while answering the safety objection.

lessons.lesson_title: Timed Q3 practice and rubric review
lessons.learning_objective: I can write and score a 40-minute argument essay using the 6-point rubric.
lessons.key_concepts: Planning in five minutes; writing to the rubric; Row B 4-point descriptor (specific evidence supports all claims, commentary consistently explains it).
lessons.key_vocabulary: plan, outline, rubric, commentary, timed, revise
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students skip planning to start writing sooner and end up with a thesis that drifts from the body.
lessons.real_world_hook: Timed writing like a workplace response that must be sent before a meeting.

lessons.lesson_title: Read and sort the sources
lessons.learning_objective: I can read six or seven sources quickly and sort them by the position they support.
lessons.key_concepts: Q1 task: argue a position using at least three of the provided sources (including visual or quantitative sources); sorting sources by stance and type.
lessons.key_vocabulary: source, stance, visual source, quantitative source, sort, perspective
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat the sources as facts to report rather than as voices in a debate that they must enter.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading several reviews before buying a laptop and noticing which reviewers agree.

lessons.lesson_title: Cite sources correctly
lessons.learning_objective: I can cite sources by letter or author and integrate them into my own argument.
lessons.key_concepts: Citation format: (Source A) or (Smith); at least three distinct sources required for full Row B credit; paraphrase versus quote; never letting a source make the claim for you.
lessons.key_vocabulary: citation, attribution, paraphrase, Source A, integrate, plagiarize
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students cite fewer than three sources or cite one source three times, which limits Row B; others summarize each source in turn instead of using them.
lessons.real_world_hook: Crediting sources correctly in a school newspaper article.

lessons.lesson_title: Put sources in conversation
lessons.learning_objective: I can make sources talk to each other to support and complicate my argument.
lessons.key_concepts: Source-to-source synthesis; agreement, tension, and qualification across sources; my voice leading the argument; source-by-source summary as a trap.
lessons.key_vocabulary: synthesize, tension, corroborate, complicate, conversation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write one paragraph per source, producing a summary, rather than organizing by claims that draw on several sources.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing what two experts on a news panel actually disagree about.

lessons.lesson_title: Timed synthesis practice
lessons.learning_objective: I can use the reading period and write a full synthesis essay in about 40 minutes.
lessons.key_concepts: 15-minute reading period; planning a position and grouping sources; Row C opportunities such as exploring tensions across sources or wider implications.
lessons.key_vocabulary: reading period, plan, position, implication, tension, timed
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students spend most of the reading period rereading every source closely and run out of time to plan.
lessons.real_world_hook: Preparing a briefing for a decision-maker from a stack of reports in under an hour.

lessons.lesson_title: Diction and tone
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how a writer's word choice creates tone and serves purpose.
lessons.key_concepts: Diction (connotation, specificity, register); tone and shifts in tone; how word choice shapes audience response.
lessons.key_vocabulary: diction, connotation, tone, register, shift, nuance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students describe tone with vague words like "emotional" or "negative" instead of precise words such as "wry" or "indignant."
lessons.real_world_hook: Noticing how a news outlet calls the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters."

lessons.lesson_title: Syntax and sentence craft
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain and use syntax such as parallelism, periodic sentences, and short sentences for emphasis.
lessons.key_concepts: Clause placement (independent and dependent); parallelism; periodic and cumulative sentences; sentence length and rhythm for emphasis; punctuation as a style choice.
lessons.key_vocabulary: syntax, parallelism, periodic sentence, cumulative sentence, clause, emphasis
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think syntax analysis means saying a sentence is "long" or "short" without explaining the effect on meaning.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analyzing why "I came, I saw, I conquered" sticks.

lessons.lesson_title: Earn the sophistication point
lessons.learning_objective: I can build complexity into my argument to earn Row C.
lessons.key_concepts: Row C (0-1): complexity must be part of the argument itself; ways to earn it include exploring tensions, explaining wider implications or significance, situating the argument in a broader context, and a consistently vivid and persuasive style.
lessons.key_vocabulary: sophistication, complexity, implication, tension, broader context, nuance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students try to earn sophistication by adding big vocabulary or a single "some may argue" sentence; Row C is the least-earned point and requires sustained complexity.
lessons.real_world_hook: Watching how a strong columnist widens a local story into a national issue.

lessons.lesson_title: Revise for clarity and voice
lessons.learning_objective: I can revise sentences for concision, precision, and a consistent voice.
lessons.key_concepts: Concision; strong verbs; eliminating wordiness and vague words; purposeful punctuation (dashes, colons, semicolons); consistent voice.
lessons.key_vocabulary: concision, wordiness, voice, precise, revise, punctuation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students believe formal writing means longer words and more passive voice.
lessons.real_world_hook: Cutting a 300-word email to 120 words so a busy reader actually reads it.

units.unit_title: Multiple choice: reading and composition questions

lessons.lesson_title: Reading questions on nonfiction passages
lessons.learning_objective: I can answer reading questions about purpose, audience, claims, organization, and style.
lessons.key_concepts: About 23-25 reading questions on nonfiction passages; question stems (primary purpose, function of a paragraph, effect of a word); line references.
lessons.key_vocabulary: primary purpose, function, rhetorical effect, line reference, stem
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students pick answers that are true about the passage but do not answer the specific question asked.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a policy memo carefully enough to answer your manager's specific question.

lessons.lesson_title: Composition (revision) questions
lessons.learning_objective: I can answer writing questions about adding, deleting, revising, and reordering sentences.
lessons.key_concepts: About 20-22 writing questions on draft passages: should the writer add or delete a sentence, which choice best strengthens a claim, which transition fits, which conclusion fits the purpose.
lessons.key_vocabulary: revise, delete, add, strengthen, transition, purpose
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose the most interesting or detailed sentence instead of the one that best serves the writer's stated purpose.
lessons.real_world_hook: Giving useful edit suggestions on a classmate's college essay.

lessons.lesson_title: Eliminate wrong answers efficiently
lessons.learning_objective: I can eliminate distractors that are too broad, too extreme, or off purpose.
lessons.key_concepts: Common distractor patterns (half-right, too extreme, true but irrelevant, wrong part of the passage); returning to the text; pacing across 45 questions in about one hour.
lessons.key_vocabulary: distractor, eliminate, extreme, half-right, pacing
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose answers based on memory of the passage rather than rechecking the referenced lines.
lessons.real_world_hook: Spotting the misleading option in a multiple-choice survey or contract summary.

lessons.lesson_title: Plan the exam day
lessons.learning_objective: I can describe the AP Lang exam format and plan my time for each section.
lessons.key_concepts: Digital exam in Bluebook, 3 hours 15 minutes; 45 MC questions (45%); 3 essays (55%) in 2 hours 15 minutes including a 15-minute reading period; about 40 minutes per essay; essays can be written in any order.
lessons.key_vocabulary: Bluebook, reading period, pacing, section, weight
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume they must write the essays in order (Q1, Q2, Q3) and lose time on the one they find hardest.
lessons.real_world_hook: Planning a high-stakes day like a job interview with a clear schedule.

lessons.lesson_title: Five-minute planning routine
lessons.learning_objective: I can plan any AP Lang essay in about five minutes with a thesis and a line of reasoning.
lessons.key_concepts: Quick plan: decode the prompt, write the thesis first, list two or three claims with evidence, note one complexity move for Row C.
lessons.key_vocabulary: plan, outline, thesis-first, claim, complexity
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think planning wastes time; unplanned essays often drift and lose the thesis and Row B points.
lessons.real_world_hook: Sketching talking points before a debate rebuttal.

lessons.lesson_title: Full timed practice and self-scoring
lessons.learning_objective: I can complete a timed essay set and score it against the 1-4-1 rubric to find my next goal.
lessons.key_concepts: Self-scoring with rubric rows; identifying the weakest row; setting one targeted revision goal; recent FRQ mean scores near 3.3-3.6 out of 6 as a benchmark.
lessons.key_vocabulary: self-assessment, rubric row, benchmark, goal, revision
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students judge an essay by how it feels to write rather than by whether each rubric row is met.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reviewing game film after a match to fix one specific weakness.

units.unit_title: Short fiction I: character, setting, and plot

lessons.lesson_title: Characters revealed through details
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how specific textual details reveal a character's perspective, motives, and values.
lessons.key_concepts: Characterization through action, dialogue, thought, and description; direct versus indirect characterization; inferring motives.
lessons.prerequisites: Analyzing how characters develop over a text.
lessons.key_vocabulary: characterization, direct, indirect, motive, perspective, values
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students describe what a character does (plot summary) instead of interpreting what the details reveal.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a short story like Kate Chopin's "The Story of an Hour" and inferring what the main character really feels.

lessons.lesson_title: Setting as more than backdrop
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how setting shapes characters and creates mood and meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Setting as time, place, and social environment; setting reflecting or contrasting a character's values; mood.
lessons.key_vocabulary: setting, mood, atmosphere, environment, values, contrast
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat setting as background scenery and never connect it to character or theme.
lessons.real_world_hook: Noticing how a horror film's isolated house raises tension before anything happens.

lessons.lesson_title: Plot and the order of events
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how the sequence and structure of a plot create tension and meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Exposition, conflict, climax, resolution; flashback and foreshadowing; how structural choices shape a reader's experience.
lessons.key_vocabulary: conflict, climax, flashback, foreshadowing, pacing, structure
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students believe structure analysis means retelling the plot in order.
lessons.real_world_hook: Explaining why a TV episode opens with the ending and then flashes back.

lessons.lesson_title: Narrator and point of view
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how a narrator's point of view and reliability shape what the reader learns.
lessons.key_concepts: First, second, and third person; limited versus omniscient; narrative distance; the narrator is not the author.
lessons.key_vocabulary: narrator, point of view, omniscient, limited, narrative distance, perspective
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume the narrator is the author and that a narrator's opinions are the story's message.
lessons.real_world_hook: Hearing two friends tell different versions of the same argument.

units.unit_title: Poetry I: speaker, imagery, and form

lessons.lesson_title: Speaker and situation
lessons.learning_objective: I can identify a poem's speaker, situation, and audience.
lessons.key_concepts: The speaker is not the poet; dramatic situation; addressee; shifts in the speaker's attitude.
lessons.key_vocabulary: speaker, persona, addressee, situation, attitude, shift
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume every poem is the poet's autobiography.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a dramatic monologue like Browning's "My Last Duchess" as a performance by a character.

lessons.lesson_title: Imagery and word choice
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how imagery and diction create meaning and tone in a poem.
lessons.key_concepts: Sensory imagery; connotation; precise diction; how images accumulate into a pattern.
lessons.key_vocabulary: imagery, diction, connotation, sensory, tone, pattern
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students list images by sense (sight, sound) without explaining what the pattern of images means.
lessons.real_world_hook: Noticing how a song lyric uses one striking image to carry an entire mood.

lessons.lesson_title: Line, stanza, and form
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how line breaks, stanzas, and fixed forms contribute to meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Line breaks and enjambment; stanza; sonnet and volta; free verse; how form creates emphasis and shifts.
lessons.key_vocabulary: enjambment, stanza, sonnet, volta, free verse, caesura
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think form is decoration and ignore that a sonnet's volta often marks the poem's key turn.
lessons.real_world_hook: Seeing how a rapper's line breaks set up a punchline.

lessons.lesson_title: Paraphrase before you analyze
lessons.learning_objective: I can paraphrase a difficult poem literally before interpreting it.
lessons.key_concepts: Sentence-by-sentence paraphrase; unpacking inverted syntax; distinguishing literal meaning from figurative meaning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: paraphrase, literal, figurative, syntax, inversion
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students jump to a hidden meaning before understanding what the poem literally says.
lessons.real_world_hook: Translating a dense Shakespearean line into plain English before discussing it.

lessons.lesson_title: Character arcs across a long work
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how a character changes or stays the same across a novel or play and why it matters.
lessons.key_concepts: Dynamic and static characters; turning points; how change or lack of change develops meaning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: dynamic, static, arc, turning point, epiphany
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume every main character must change, overlooking that a static character can be the point.
lessons.real_world_hook: Tracing Jay Gatsby's refusal to let go of the past in The Great Gatsby.

lessons.lesson_title: Foils and contrasting characters
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how contrasting characters illuminate each other and the work's meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Foil characters; contrast of values; how a minor character sharpens a major one.
lessons.prerequisites: Character arcs across a long work.
lessons.key_vocabulary: foil, contrast, values, minor character, illuminate
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students describe two characters separately and never explain what the contrast reveals.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing Hamlet and Laertes as sons avenging their fathers.

lessons.lesson_title: Dramatic structure and conventions
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how dramatic conventions like soliloquy, aside, and dramatic irony shape a play.
lessons.key_concepts: Acts and scenes; soliloquy; aside; dramatic irony; stage directions; tragic structure.
lessons.prerequisites: Plot and the order of events.
lessons.key_vocabulary: soliloquy, aside, dramatic irony, stage directions, tragedy, act
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students read plays as novels and ignore what the audience knows that characters do not.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analyzing why the audience squirms when they know the twist before the character does.

lessons.lesson_title: Track a big idea through a whole work
lessons.learning_objective: I can track how a symbol, conflict, or idea develops across a full novel or play.
lessons.key_concepts: Recurring motifs and symbols; developing a theme over time; noting evidence across chapters or acts.
lessons.prerequisites: Character arcs across a long work.
lessons.key_vocabulary: motif, symbol, theme, recurrence, development
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students state a theme as a single word ("love") instead of a claim about it.
lessons.real_world_hook: Tracking the green light across The Great Gatsby.

units.unit_title: Short fiction II: complexity and ambiguity

lessons.lesson_title: Unreliable narrators
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how an unreliable narrator creates irony and shapes interpretation.
lessons.key_concepts: Unreliability through bias, limited knowledge, or self-deception; gaps between what the narrator says and what the reader sees; irony.
lessons.key_vocabulary: unreliable narrator, irony, bias, self-deception, gap
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students take a narrator's account at face value and miss the irony that drives the story.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart" and noticing the narrator insisting he is sane.

lessons.lesson_title: Characters with competing values
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how a character's internal conflicts and competing values create complexity.
lessons.key_concepts: Internal conflict; contradictory motives; ambiguity in characterization; resisting simple good-or-bad labels.
lessons.key_vocabulary: internal conflict, contradiction, ambiguity, complexity, motive
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students label characters as heroes or villains instead of analyzing their contradictions.
lessons.real_world_hook: Debating whether a character in a streaming drama is sympathetic or manipulative.

lessons.lesson_title: Endings and ambiguity
lessons.learning_objective: I can interpret an ambiguous or open ending using textual evidence.
lessons.key_concepts: Open endings; ambiguity as a deliberate choice; multiple defensible interpretations supported by evidence.
lessons.prerequisites: Plot and the order of events.
lessons.key_vocabulary: ambiguity, open ending, resolution, interpretation, defensible
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think an ambiguous ending means any interpretation is valid, even one the text does not support.
lessons.real_world_hook: Arguing about the final scene of a film that cuts to black.

lessons.lesson_title: From observation to interpretation
lessons.learning_objective: I can move from noticing a detail to writing an interpretive claim about its significance.
lessons.key_concepts: Observation, then pattern, then interpretation; interpretive claims answer "how" and "why," not "what".
lessons.key_vocabulary: observation, pattern, interpretation, significance, claim
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write plot summary instead of interpretation, the most common reason literary essays score low.
lessons.real_world_hook: Moving from "the room is dark" to what the darkness says about the character.

units.unit_title: Poetry II: figurative language and sound

lessons.lesson_title: Metaphor and simile as comparison
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how a metaphor or simile transfers qualities from one thing to another to create meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Tenor and vehicle; transferred qualities; extended metaphor; conceit.
lessons.key_vocabulary: metaphor, simile, tenor, vehicle, extended metaphor, conceit
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students identify a metaphor but do not explain which qualities carry over and why.
lessons.real_world_hook: Unpacking John Donne's compass comparison in "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning."

lessons.lesson_title: Personification, allusion, and symbol
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how personification, allusion, and symbols add layers of meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Personification; allusion to myth, scripture, or history; symbol versus image; context from allusions.
lessons.key_vocabulary: personification, allusion, symbol, connotation, layered meaning
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume every object in a poem is a symbol, forcing meanings the text does not support.
lessons.real_world_hook: Recognizing a biblical or mythological allusion in a political speech.

lessons.lesson_title: Sound and rhythm
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how meter, rhyme, and sound devices reinforce meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Iambic pentameter and variations; rhyme scheme; alliteration, assonance, consonance; sound reinforcing sense.
lessons.key_vocabulary: meter, iambic pentameter, rhyme scheme, alliteration, assonance, consonance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students identify a rhyme scheme and stop there instead of explaining what it emphasizes or disrupts.
lessons.real_world_hook: Hearing how a song's rhythm shifts when the singer's mood changes.

lessons.lesson_title: Shifts and tone in poetry
lessons.learning_objective: I can identify shifts in a poem and explain how they change its tone or meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Shifts signaled by words like "but" and "yet," stanza breaks, or the volta; tone before and after the shift.
lessons.prerequisites: Speaker and situation; sound and rhythm.
lessons.key_vocabulary: shift, volta, tone, contrast, turn, attitude
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students describe a poem's tone as one fixed word and miss the turn that drives the poem.
lessons.real_world_hook: Noticing the turn in Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 from mockery to sincere love.

lessons.lesson_title: Narrative perspective in the novel
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how a novelist's choice of narrator and perspective shapes a reader's understanding.
lessons.key_concepts: Frame narratives; multiple narrators; shifting perspectives; narrative distance.
lessons.key_vocabulary: frame narrative, multiple narrators, perspective, narrative distance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students ignore how a frame narrative (such as the nested narrators of Frankenstein) shapes what the reader can trust.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing Walton, Victor, and the Creature as narrators in Frankenstein.

lessons.lesson_title: Setting, society, and power
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how the setting of a novel or play reflects the values and power structures of a society.
lessons.key_concepts: Social and historical setting; power structures; how characters conform to or resist their environment.
lessons.key_vocabulary: society, power, conform, resist, historical context
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat historical setting as background trivia rather than as a force acting on characters.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analyzing Okonkwo's village and the arrival of colonizers in Things Fall Apart.

lessons.lesson_title: Structure across a novel
lessons.learning_objective: I can explain how chapter order, time shifts, and parallel plots develop meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Nonlinear structure; parallel plots; juxtaposition of chapters; withholding information.
lessons.prerequisites: Plot and the order of events.
