lessons.key_concepts: Semicolon joins two independent clauses (or separates complex list items); colon follows an independent clause to introduce a list, explanation, or example.
lessons.key_vocabulary: semicolon, colon, independent clause, list, explanation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students put a colon after an incomplete clause ("The ingredients are: flour") or use a semicolon before a fragment.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing clear instructions with a list.

lessons.lesson_title: Dashes and nonessential elements
lessons.learning_objective: I can punctuate nonessential elements with matching commas, dashes, or parentheses.
lessons.ccss_code: SAT RW Standard English Conventions / L.11-12.2
lessons.key_concepts: Nonessential (extra) information set off with matching punctuation; do not mix a comma with a dash; essential elements take no commas.
lessons.key_vocabulary: dash, nonessential, essential, appositive, parentheses
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students open an interrupter with a dash and close it with a comma.
lessons.real_world_hook: Adding a side comment in a professional email.

lessons.lesson_title: Commas with introductory elements and lists
lessons.learning_objective: I can place commas correctly after introductory elements, in lists, and avoid unnecessary commas.
lessons.ccss_code: SAT RW Standard English Conventions / L.11-12.2
lessons.key_concepts: Comma after introductory phrases and clauses; commas in a series; no comma between subject and verb or between a verb and its object.
lessons.key_vocabulary: introductory phrase, series, subject, verb, unnecessary comma
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students place a comma between a long subject and its verb.
lessons.real_world_hook: Proofreading a scholarship essay.

units.unit_title: Standard English Conventions: form, structure, and sense

lessons.lesson_title: Subject-verb agreement
lessons.learning_objective: I can make verbs agree with their subjects, even when phrases separate them.
lessons.ccss_code: SAT RW Standard English Conventions / L.11-12.1
lessons.key_concepts: Find the true subject; ignore prepositional phrases and interrupters; collective nouns; each and every as singular.
lessons.key_vocabulary: subject, verb, agreement, prepositional phrase, collective noun
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students make the verb agree with the nearest noun ("The list of items are").
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a grammatically correct product description.

lessons.lesson_title: Pronouns and possessives
lessons.learning_objective: I can use pronouns that agree with their antecedents and distinguish possessives from contractions and plurals.
lessons.ccss_code: SAT RW Standard English Conventions / L.11-12.1
lessons.key_concepts: Pronoun-antecedent agreement in number; its versus it's; their versus they're; singular and plural possessives (student's, students').
lessons.key_vocabulary: pronoun, antecedent, possessive, contraction, plural
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use "their" for a singular collective noun like "the company" or confuse its and it's.
lessons.real_world_hook: Proofreading a company's social media post.

lessons.lesson_title: Verb tense and form
lessons.learning_objective: I can choose verb tenses that are consistent and logical within a passage.
lessons.ccss_code: SAT RW Standard English Conventions / L.11-12.1
lessons.key_concepts: Tense consistency with surrounding verbs; past, present, and present perfect; finite verbs needed for a complete sentence.
lessons.key_vocabulary: tense, consistency, present perfect, finite verb, fragment
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose a tense based on what sounds right without checking the tense of nearby verbs.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a résumé with consistent verb tenses.

lessons.lesson_title: Modifiers and sentence sense
lessons.learning_objective: I can fix dangling and misplaced modifiers so they clearly describe the right word.
lessons.ccss_code: SAT RW Standard English Conventions / L.11-12.1
lessons.key_concepts: An introductory modifier must be followed immediately by the noun it describes; misplaced modifiers; logical sentence structure.
lessons.key_vocabulary: modifier, dangling, misplaced, introductory phrase, subject
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose the answer that sounds smooth even when the modifier describes the wrong noun.
lessons.real_world_hook: Fixing a funny caption like "Running for the bus, my backpack fell."

units.unit_title: Test strategy, adaptive modules, and pacing

lessons.lesson_title: How the digital SAT RW section works
lessons.learning_objective: I can describe the digital SAT Reading and Writing format and how adaptive modules work.
lessons.key_concepts: 54 questions in two 32-minute modules of 27 questions; one short passage per question; module 2 is easier or harder depending on module 1 performance; scored 200-800; taken in Bluebook.
lessons.key_vocabulary: module, adaptive, Bluebook, scaled score, section
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think every question is worth the same and that a harder second module means they are doing badly; it actually signals strong module 1 performance.
lessons.real_world_hook: Understanding how a video game adjusts its difficulty.

lessons.lesson_title: Pacing at about 71 seconds per question
lessons.learning_objective: I can pace myself at about 71 seconds per question and decide when to move on.
lessons.key_concepts: 32 minutes / 27 questions is about 71 seconds each; quick wins first; mark for review; no penalty for guessing, so never leave a blank.
lessons.prerequisites: How the digital SAT RW section works.
lessons.key_vocabulary: pacing, mark for review, guess, time management, skip
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students spend three minutes on one hard question and rush the last five.
lessons.real_world_hook: Managing time on a timed online application.

lessons.lesson_title: Question types and order
lessons.learning_objective: I can recognize each question type quickly and apply the right strategy.
lessons.key_concepts: Questions are grouped by type and similar questions are ordered from easier to harder; predict-then-match; goal-first for notes questions; rule-first for conventions.
lessons.prerequisites: Pacing at about 71 seconds per question.
lessons.key_vocabulary: question type, predict, match, strategy, grouping
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use the same slow, read-everything approach for every question type.
lessons.real_world_hook: Using the right tool for each job.

lessons.lesson_title: Practice test review
lessons.learning_objective: I can review a practice test to find error patterns and plan targeted practice.
lessons.key_concepts: Error log by domain and skill; careless versus content errors; targeted practice on the weakest skills; Bluebook full-length practice tests.
lessons.key_vocabulary: error log, pattern, careless error, domain, targeted practice
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students take practice test after practice test without reviewing why they missed questions.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reviewing game film to improve.

lessons.lesson_title: How the ACT English and Reading tests work
lessons.learning_objective: I can describe the format, timing, and scoring of the enhanced ACT English and Reading tests.
lessons.key_concepts: Enhanced ACT (online from April 2025, paper from September 2025 for national testing): English is 50 questions in 35 minutes, Reading is 36 questions in 40 minutes; Math is 45 questions in 50 minutes. Science (40 questions, 40 minutes) and Writing (one essay, 40 minutes) are optional. The Composite (1-36) is the average of English, math, and reading only; Science feeds a STEM score instead. Each section includes embedded unscored field-test questions you cannot identify, so treat every question as scored. English reports Production of Writing (38-43%), Knowledge of Language (18-23%), and Conventions of Standard English (38-43%); Reading reports Key Ideas and Details (44-52%), Craft and Structure (26-33%), and Integration of Knowledge and Ideas (19-26%). Reading includes some paired shorter passages and may include a graph, table, or figure. No penalty for wrong answers.
lessons.prerequisites: Basic familiarity with multiple-choice reading and grammar questions.
lessons.key_vocabulary: Composite score, scale score, reporting category, field-test question, optional section, superscore, NO CHANGE
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students still think the Composite averages four sections and that skipping Science lowers it, when the enhanced Composite uses only English, math, and reading.
lessons.real_world_hook: Planning which optional sections to take based on what the colleges on your list actually require.

lessons.lesson_title: Set a baseline and a target
lessons.learning_objective: I can take a diagnostic, read my score report by reporting category, and set a realistic target score.
lessons.key_concepts: Timed diagnostic under real conditions; reading category scores to find the weakest area; target score from college middle-50% ranges; an error log (question type, why missed, fix).
lessons.prerequisites: How the ACT English and Reading tests work.
lessons.key_vocabulary: diagnostic, error log, middle 50% range, reporting category, careless error, content gap
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students take the diagnostic untimed or with breaks, then plan around a score that overstates their real-time performance.
lessons.real_world_hook: Looking up the ACT range of admitted students at a target college and planning study weeks backward from the test date.

lessons.lesson_title: Topic development: add, delete, or keep
lessons.learning_objective: I can decide whether a sentence should be added or deleted by judging its relevance to the paragraph's focus.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT English: Production of Writing / W.11-12.2b
lessons.key_concepts: Questions ask "Should the writer add/delete this sentence?" Answer Yes/No first based on relevance to the paragraph's main point, then choose the reason that accurately describes the sentence; true or interesting is not the same as relevant.
lessons.prerequisites: Identifying the main idea of a paragraph.
lessons.key_vocabulary: relevance, focus, main idea, digression, supporting detail
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose "Yes, because it provides interesting details" whenever the sentence is accurate and vivid, even though it drifts off the paragraph's topic.
lessons.real_world_hook: Cutting a fun but off-topic fact from a scholarship essay so the paragraph stays focused.

lessons.lesson_title: Purpose and goal questions
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine whether a passage or sentence accomplishes a stated purpose.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT English: Production of Writing / W.11-12.4
lessons.key_concepts: "Suppose the writer's goal was to..." questions; restate the goal in your own words, then test the passage against it; the reason must match what the essay actually does.
lessons.prerequisites: Topic development: add, delete, or keep.
lessons.key_vocabulary: purpose, goal, primary focus, accomplish, rhetorical aim
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students answer goal questions based on whether they liked the essay or whether it mentions the topic at all, rather than whether it fulfills the specific goal stated (e.g., "to explain the history of" vs. one person's experience).
lessons.real_world_hook: Checking whether a cover letter actually shows what the job posting asked for.

lessons.lesson_title: Organization: placing sentences and paragraphs
lessons.learning_objective: I can place a sentence or paragraph in its most logical position using pronouns, time cues, and topic links.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT English: Production of Writing / W.11-12.2a
lessons.key_concepts: Logical order; clues in pronouns ("this," "they"), time words, and repeated nouns; a sentence must follow the idea it refers back to; introductions and conclusions frame the essay.
lessons.prerequisites: Identifying the main idea of a paragraph.
lessons.key_vocabulary: sequence, logical order, cohesion, referent, introduction, conclusion
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students place a sentence that begins with "This discovery" before the sentence that describes the discovery.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reordering steps in a recipe or instructions so each step makes sense after the one before it.

lessons.lesson_title: Transitions and logical connectors
lessons.learning_objective: I can choose the transition word or phrase that shows the correct relationship between ideas.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT English: Production of Writing / L.11-12.1
lessons.key_concepts: Identify the relationship first: contrast (however, nevertheless), cause-effect (therefore, as a result), addition (furthermore), example (for instance), sequence (then, finally); sometimes no transition is best.
lessons.key_vocabulary: transition, contrast, cause and effect, continuation, conjunctive adverb
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students pick a sophisticated-sounding transition like "Consequently" when the second sentence actually contrasts with the first.
lessons.real_world_hook: Linking ideas clearly in an email that explains why a deadline must change.

lessons.lesson_title: Concision and redundancy
lessons.learning_objective: I can eliminate wordy and redundant phrasing while keeping the meaning.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT English: Knowledge of Language / L.11-12.3
lessons.key_concepts: Redundancy ("past history," "annually each year"); wordiness; the shortest grammatically correct choice that keeps the full meaning is often right, and OMIT is a real option.
lessons.key_vocabulary: concision, redundancy, wordiness, OMIT, precision
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students pick the longest answer because it "sounds more academic," such as "due to the fact that" instead of "because."
lessons.real_world_hook: Trimming a text or social post to fit a character limit without losing the message.

lessons.lesson_title: Precise word choice
lessons.learning_objective: I can choose the word that is most precise and appropriate in context.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT English: Knowledge of Language / L.11-12.5b
lessons.key_concepts: Denotation vs. connotation; commonly confused words (affect/effect, than/then, accept/except); idiomatic prepositions ("capable of," not "capable to"); vague words versus specific ones.
lessons.key_vocabulary: denotation, connotation, idiom, precision, diction
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose a word with the right dictionary meaning but the wrong connotation, such as calling a careful scientist "cheap" instead of "thrifty" with lab supplies.
lessons.real_world_hook: Choosing words in a review or recommendation so the tone isn't accidentally insulting.

lessons.lesson_title: Style and tone consistency
lessons.learning_objective: I can keep style and tone consistent with the rest of a passage.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT English: Knowledge of Language / L.11-12.3
lessons.key_concepts: Match the passage's register; avoid slang in formal essays and stiff jargon in casual narratives; consistent verb tense and point of view as part of style.
lessons.key_vocabulary: tone, register, formal, informal, style, consistency
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students accept a slang choice like "totally freaked out" in an otherwise formal historical essay because it is grammatically correct.
lessons.real_world_hook: Switching between texting friends and emailing a teacher without mixing registers.

units.unit_title: ACT English: Conventions of Standard English

lessons.lesson_title: Sentence boundaries: fragments, run-ons, comma splices
lessons.learning_objective: I can identify and correct fragments, run-ons, and comma splices.
lessons.key_concepts: Independent clause needs subject plus finite verb; join independent clauses with period, semicolon, or comma plus FANBOYS; subordinate clauses and -ing phrases cannot stand alone.
lessons.key_vocabulary: independent clause, dependent clause, fragment, comma splice, run-on, FANBOYS
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students fix a comma splice by swapping the comma for "however," creating another comma splice ("It rained, however we played").
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing your own text messages and essays so readers can tell where each thought ends.

lessons.lesson_title: Commas: essential and nonessential elements
lessons.learning_objective: I can use commas correctly with nonessential elements, introductory elements, and items in a series, and remove unnecessary commas.
lessons.key_concepts: Matching commas around nonessential phrases; no commas around essential (restrictive) information; comma after introductory element; no comma between subject and verb or verb and object.
lessons.key_vocabulary: nonessential, restrictive, appositive, introductory element, series comma
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students put a comma between a long subject and its verb ("The students who stayed after school, won the contest").
lessons.real_world_hook: Punctuating a name and title correctly in a news article ("Ms. Lee, the principal, said...").

lessons.lesson_title: Semicolons, colons, dashes, and apostrophes
lessons.learning_objective: I can use semicolons, colons, dashes, and apostrophes correctly.
lessons.key_concepts: Semicolon = period between independent clauses; colon after a complete clause introduces a list or explanation; matching dashes for interruptions; apostrophes for possession (singular 's, plural s') and contractions, never for plurals.
lessons.key_vocabulary: semicolon, colon, dash, apostrophe, possessive, contraction
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students put a colon directly after a verb or preposition ("The ingredients are: flour, sugar, and eggs").
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing product descriptions and lists that look professional.

lessons.lesson_title: Usage: agreement, pronouns, verbs, and modifiers
lessons.learning_objective: I can correct errors in subject-verb agreement, pronoun case and agreement, verb tense, and modifier placement.
lessons.key_concepts: Ignore prepositional phrases to find the subject; pronoun case (who/whom, I/me); pronoun must have a clear singular or plural antecedent; consistent tense; adjective vs. adverb; dangling modifiers.
lessons.key_vocabulary: agreement, antecedent, pronoun case, tense, modifier, dangling modifier
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students make the verb agree with the nearest noun ("The box of crayons are") rather than the true subject.
lessons.real_world_hook: Proofreading a group project slide where someone wrote "Each of the members have".

lessons.lesson_title: Sentence structure: parallelism and logical comparisons
lessons.learning_objective: I can fix faulty parallelism, illogical comparisons, and shifts in construction.
lessons.key_concepts: Items in a list or paired construction (not only...but also, either...or) take the same grammatical form; compare like with like ("Her score was higher than Jake's," not "than Jake").
lessons.prerequisites: Usage: agreement, pronouns, verbs, and modifiers.
lessons.key_vocabulary: parallel structure, correlative conjunction, comparison, shift, construction
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write lists like "She likes hiking, to swim, and biking" and don't hear the mismatch.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing résumé bullet points that all start with the same verb form.

lessons.lesson_title: Main idea and central claim
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine the central idea of a passage or paragraph.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT Reading: Key Ideas and Details / RI.11-12.2
lessons.key_concepts: Central idea vs. topic; read the first and last paragraphs closely; the right answer covers the whole passage, not one paragraph; too-broad and too-narrow traps.
lessons.key_vocabulary: central idea, main idea, topic, summary, scope
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose an answer that is true and mentioned in the passage but describes only one paragraph's detail, not the whole passage.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a one-sentence summary of a long article for a group chat.

lessons.lesson_title: Locating details and inferences
lessons.learning_objective: I can find stated details quickly and make inferences supported by the text.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT Reading: Key Ideas and Details / RI.11-12.1
lessons.key_concepts: Line and paragraph references; scan for key nouns; inference = what the text strongly supports, not a leap; prove every answer with words from the passage.
lessons.key_vocabulary: detail, inference, textual evidence, support, paraphrase
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students pick an inference that sounds reasonable from real-world knowledge but is never supported by the passage.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a lease or terms of service and figuring out what it implies about fees.

lessons.lesson_title: Relationships: cause-effect, comparison, sequence
lessons.learning_objective: I can identify cause-effect, comparison, and sequence relationships in a passage.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT Reading: Key Ideas and Details / RI.11-12.3
lessons.key_concepts: Signal words (because, led to, unlike, before); reversed cause-effect traps; tracking order of events in narratives that use flashback.
lessons.key_vocabulary: cause, effect, comparison, contrast, sequence, chronology, flashback
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students reverse cause and effect, answering that the drought was caused by crop failure when the passage says the drought caused the failure.
lessons.real_world_hook: Following a news story about what actually triggered a supply shortage.

lessons.lesson_title: Characters and narrators in literary passages
lessons.learning_objective: I can infer characters' motivations, relationships, and the narrator's perspective in literary passages.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT Reading: Key Ideas and Details / RL.11-12.3
lessons.key_concepts: Inferring feelings from actions and dialogue; first-person vs. third-person narrators; a narrator looking back on youth (retrospective narrator); shifts in a relationship across the passage.
lessons.key_vocabulary: narrator, point of view, motivation, characterization, retrospective
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume the narrator's opinions are the author's or the "correct" view, missing that the narrator may be biased or later change their mind.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading between the lines of a friend's story about a conflict to understand how each person felt.

lessons.lesson_title: Words and phrases in context
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine the meaning of a word or phrase as it is used in a passage.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT Reading: Craft and Structure / RI.11-12.4
lessons.key_concepts: Context clues; cover the word and predict a replacement; common words with uncommon meanings ("check" as restrain); figurative and connotative meaning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: context clue, connotation, figurative language, secondary meaning
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose the most common dictionary meaning of the word (e.g., "grave" = burial place) without testing it in the sentence.
lessons.real_world_hook: Figuring out unfamiliar jargon in a new job's training manual.

lessons.lesson_title: Author's purpose and point of view
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine the purpose of a passage, paragraph, or detail and the author's point of view.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT Reading: Craft and Structure / RI.11-12.6
lessons.key_concepts: Function questions ("the main purpose of the third paragraph is to"); verbs like illustrate, contrast, introduce, qualify; author's attitude ranges (admiring, skeptical, ambivalent); extreme answers are usually wrong.
lessons.key_vocabulary: purpose, function, point of view, attitude, tone, qualify
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students describe what a paragraph says instead of what it does, picking a summary when the question asks for the paragraph's function.
lessons.real_world_hook: Noticing when a "news" article is actually trying to persuade you.

lessons.lesson_title: Text structure and narrative technique
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyze how a passage is organized and how structural choices affect meaning.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT Reading: Craft and Structure / RL.11-12.5
lessons.key_concepts: Overall structure (chronological, problem-solution, compare-contrast, claim-counterclaim); shifts in focus or time; how an opening anecdote sets up an argument.
lessons.prerequisites: Author's purpose and point of view.
lessons.key_vocabulary: structure, shift, anecdote, flashback, problem-solution, organization
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students describe a passage's structure as "chronological" just because it contains dates, even when it is organized as a comparison.
lessons.real_world_hook: Seeing why a TED talk opens with a personal story before giving data.

units.unit_title: ACT Reading: Integration of Knowledge & Ideas

lessons.lesson_title: Paired passages
lessons.learning_objective: I can compare two related passages and answer questions about how their ideas relate.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT Reading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas / RI.11-12.9
lessons.key_concepts: Read Passage A and answer its questions, then Passage B and its questions, then the questions about both; relationships: agree, disagree, extend, give an example of; the answer must be true of both passages.
lessons.key_vocabulary: paired passages, synthesis, compare, contrast, perspective
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students answer a "both passages" question with a statement that is true of only one passage.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing two reviews of the same phone to decide whether they actually disagree.

lessons.lesson_title: Arguments, claims, and evidence
lessons.learning_objective: I can evaluate how an author supports a claim and distinguish claims from evidence.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT Reading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas / RI.11-12.8
lessons.key_concepts: Claim vs. evidence vs. opinion; what kind of support is offered (data, expert, anecdote); which statement would strengthen or best support a claim.
lessons.key_vocabulary: claim, evidence, support, reasoning, fact, opinion
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose evidence that is on the same topic as the claim but doesn't actually support the specific point being made.
lessons.real_world_hook: Judging whether an ad's testimonial really proves the product works.

lessons.lesson_title: Visual and quantitative information
lessons.learning_objective: I can interpret a graph, table, or figure with a passage and connect it to the text.
lessons.ccss_code: ACT Reading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas / RI.11-12.7
lessons.key_concepts: Read titles, axes, and units first; identify what the graphic shows; check whether the passage and graphic agree; avoid claims beyond the data.
lessons.key_vocabulary: axis, trend, data, units, correlation, figure
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students read the trend correctly but pick an answer that claims the graph proves cause, when it only shows a correlation.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a chart in a news article about prices or screen time without overreaching.

units.unit_title: Pacing, strategy, and the optional Writing test

lessons.lesson_title: English pacing and strategy
lessons.learning_objective: I can pace the English test at about 42 seconds per question and apply a consistent elimination method.
lessons.key_concepts: 35 minutes / 50 questions is about 42 seconds each; read the whole sentence, not just the underlined part; identify the error type from what changes across choices; shortest correct answer; NO CHANGE is a legitimate choice and is sometimes correct.
lessons.prerequisites: Conventions and Production of Writing lessons.
lessons.key_vocabulary: pacing, elimination, error type, NO CHANGE, shortest answer
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students never choose NO CHANGE because they assume every underlined portion contains an error.
lessons.real_world_hook: Proofreading under time pressure, like checking an application before a deadline.

lessons.lesson_title: Reading pacing and passage strategy
lessons.learning_objective: I can pace the Reading test at about 10 minutes per passage set and choose an approach that fits me.
lessons.key_concepts: 40 minutes / 36 questions; about 10 minutes per passage set; skim-then-answer vs. read-then-answer; do your strongest passage type first; answer line-reference questions first; guess and move on.
lessons.prerequisites: Key Ideas & Details, Craft & Structure, and Integration lessons.
lessons.key_vocabulary: pacing, skim, line reference, passage set, triage
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students spend 15 minutes on the first passage trying to understand every sentence and then guess blindly on the last one.
lessons.real_world_hook: Budgeting time on any timed task, like a work shift with several deadlines.

lessons.lesson_title: The optional ACT Writing essay
lessons.learning_objective: I can plan and write an argumentative essay that takes a position and engages with the given perspectives in 40 minutes.
lessons.key_concepts: One 40-minute essay on an issue with three given perspectives; state your own position and relate it to at least one perspective; scored on Ideas and Analysis, Development and Support, Organization, and Language Use and Conventions; score 2-12, reported separately and not part of the Composite. Plan about 8 minutes, write about 28, proofread about 4.
lessons.prerequisites: Writing claims with evidence and counterargument.
lessons.key_vocabulary: perspective, position, counterargument, development, analysis, domain score
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students just summarize the three perspectives one by one without ever taking and defending their own position.
lessons.real_world_hook: Taking a clear stance in a debate or a town-hall comment while acknowledging other views.

lessons.lesson_title: Full practice test review
lessons.learning_objective: I can review a full timed practice test to find patterns in my errors and plan next steps.
lessons.key_concepts: Score by reporting category; sort misses into content gap, misread, or timing; redo missed questions untimed; plan practice on the two weakest skills; retest and compare.
lessons.key_vocabulary: error log, reporting category, content gap, timing error, retest
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students check only which answers were wrong and move on, without writing down why they chose the wrong answer.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reviewing game footage or a failed recipe to figure out what to change next time.

lessons.lesson_title: Theme and central idea in literature
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine a theme of a literary text and trace how it develops.
lessons.key_concepts: Theme as a statement about life, not one word; trace how character choices and conflicts build the theme; distinguish theme from plot summary.
lessons.key_vocabulary: theme, central idea, conflict, resolution, universal message
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students give a one-word topic ("friendship") as the theme instead of a full statement such as "True friendship requires honesty even when it hurts."
lessons.real_world_hook: Explaining what a movie is really saying about growing up.

lessons.lesson_title: Characterization and plot development
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyze how complex characters develop and advance the plot.
lessons.key_concepts: Direct and indirect characterization; motivations; how a character's choices create conflict and turning points; dynamic vs. static characters.
lessons.key_vocabulary: characterization, motivation, dynamic character, static character, conflict, turning point
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students explain a character only by what happens to them, not by the choices they make and why.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analyzing why a show's main character makes a choice fans argue about.

lessons.lesson_title: Figurative language, tone, and word choice
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyze how figurative language and word choice create tone and meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Simile, metaphor, personification, imagery; connotation shapes tone; tone words (wistful, sardonic, reverent); the effect of a word choice on the reader.
lessons.key_vocabulary: figurative language, connotation, tone, mood, imagery, diction
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students identify a metaphor but never explain what it suggests or how it affects the tone.
lessons.real_world_hook: Noticing how song lyrics use imagery to make a feeling vivid.

lessons.lesson_title: Structure, point of view, and poetry and drama
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyze how an author's structural choices and point of view shape a poem, play, or story.
lessons.key_concepts: Flashback, foreshadowing, pacing, stanza and line breaks, dramatic irony, dialogue and stage directions; first vs. third person and what the narrator knows.
lessons.prerequisites: Figurative language, tone, and word choice.
lessons.key_vocabulary: structure, flashback, foreshadowing, stanza, dramatic irony, point of view
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students say a poem's lines are broken "to make it look like a poem" instead of explaining how a break emphasizes a word or idea.
lessons.real_world_hook: Seeing how a thriller's flashback reveals a secret at just the right moment.

lessons.lesson_title: Central idea and summary of informational texts
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine the central idea of an informational text and write an objective summary.
lessons.key_concepts: Central idea vs. supporting details; objective summary leaves out opinion; how the central idea is developed across paragraphs.
lessons.prerequisites: Theme and central idea in literature.
lessons.key_vocabulary: central idea, supporting detail, objective summary, development
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students include their own opinions ("This article is very interesting") in an objective summary.
lessons.real_world_hook: Summarizing a news article fairly for someone who disagrees with it.

lessons.lesson_title: Author's purpose, point of view, and rhetoric
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine an author's purpose and point of view and analyze rhetoric used to advance it.
lessons.key_concepts: Purpose (inform, persuade, explain, entertain); point of view; rhetorical appeals and devices (repetition, rhetorical question, anecdote) as tools for purpose.
lessons.key_vocabulary: purpose, point of view, rhetoric, ethos, pathos, logos, rhetorical question
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students label an author's purpose as "to inform" for every text, even editorials clearly written to persuade.
lessons.real_world_hook: Spotting how a public-service ad tries to change behavior.

lessons.lesson_title: Text structure and text features
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyze how an author's ideas are developed by sentences, paragraphs, and text features.
lessons.key_concepts: Organizational patterns (cause-effect, problem-solution, compare-contrast, chronological); headings, captions, sidebars, graphics; how a paragraph contributes to the whole.
lessons.prerequisites: Author's purpose and point of view.
lessons.key_vocabulary: text structure, problem-solution, cause-effect, text feature, caption, heading
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students skip headings, captions, and graphics on exam passages even though questions often ask how they support the text.
lessons.real_world_hook: Using headings and diagrams to find instructions fast in a product manual.

lessons.lesson_title: Evaluating arguments and evidence
lessons.learning_objective: I can evaluate whether an argument's reasoning is valid and its evidence is relevant and sufficient.
lessons.key_concepts: Claim, reasons, evidence; relevance and sufficiency; identifying false statements and fallacious reasoning (hasty generalization, false cause, bandwagon).
lessons.prerequisites: Author's purpose, point of view, and rhetoric.
lessons.key_vocabulary: claim, evidence, relevant, sufficient, fallacy, reasoning
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat a single dramatic anecdote as sufficient evidence for a broad claim about everyone.
lessons.real_world_hook: Deciding whether an online product claim is backed by real evidence.

lessons.lesson_title: Comparing themes and topics across texts
lessons.learning_objective: I can compare how two texts treat the same theme or topic.
lessons.key_concepts: Read each text for its own central idea first; then identify similarities and differences in message, tone, and form; compare across genres (poem and story, article and memoir).
lessons.key_vocabulary: compare, contrast, paired passages, synthesis, genre
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write about each text separately without ever stating how they are alike or different.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing how a song and a novel portray the same experience of loss.

lessons.lesson_title: Comparing authors' arguments and perspectives
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyze how two authors writing about the same topic emphasize different evidence or reach different conclusions.
lessons.key_concepts: Each author's claim; what evidence each emphasizes or omits; where they agree, disagree, or talk past each other; questions phrased "both authors would agree that...".
lessons.key_vocabulary: perspective, emphasis, omission, agree, disagree, synthesis
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose a "both authors agree" answer that only one author actually states.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading two op-eds on the same school policy and figuring out where they truly differ.

lessons.lesson_title: Answering multi-part and evidence-based questions
lessons.learning_objective: I can answer two-part questions by choosing an answer and the evidence that best supports it.
lessons.key_concepts: Part A answer plus Part B evidence; the evidence must support the Part A answer specifically; use Part B choices to check Part A; strong vs. thorough textual evidence.
lessons.key_vocabulary: evidence-based selected response, Part A, Part B, textual evidence, support
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose Part B evidence that is a true quotation from the passage but doesn't prove the answer they chose in Part A.
lessons.real_world_hook: Backing up a claim in an argument with the exact quote that proves it.

lessons.lesson_title: Revising for organization and development
lessons.learning_objective: I can revise a draft by improving its introduction, transitions, supporting details, and conclusion.
lessons.key_concepts: Revision items ask which sentence best introduces or concludes, which detail best supports, or where to add a transition; judge against the paragraph's purpose.
lessons.prerequisites: Identifying central idea and supporting details.
lessons.key_vocabulary: revise, thesis, transition, supporting detail, conclusion, cohesion
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose the conclusion that introduces a brand-new idea instead of one that wraps up the essay's main point.
lessons.real_world_hook: Revising a club newsletter article so it flows from start to finish.

lessons.lesson_title: Editing sentences: boundaries and punctuation
lessons.learning_objective: I can edit sentences for fragments, run-ons, comma splices, and punctuation errors.
lessons.key_concepts: Complete sentences; semicolons between independent clauses; colons after a complete clause; commas with introductory elements and nonessential phrases.
lessons.key_vocabulary: fragment, run-on, comma splice, semicolon, colon, independent clause
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students fix a fragment by adding a comma and attaching it to the wrong sentence ("Because it rained, the game. Was canceled.").
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing an application essay before you submit it.

lessons.lesson_title: Editing for usage: agreement, pronouns, and verbs
lessons.learning_objective: I can edit for subject-verb agreement, pronoun usage, and consistent verb tense.
lessons.key_concepts: Find the true subject; indefinite pronouns (each, everyone are singular); clear pronoun antecedents; consistent tense; commonly confused words (their/there/they're).
lessons.key_vocabulary: agreement, antecedent, indefinite pronoun, tense, usage
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students change a verb to agree with a noun in a prepositional phrase ("One of the players are injured").
lessons.real_world_hook: Proofreading a job email so it sounds polished.

lessons.lesson_title: Editing for style: parallelism, concision, and word choice
lessons.learning_objective: I can edit for parallel structure, concise wording, and precise word choice.
lessons.key_concepts: Parallel lists and comparisons; removing redundancy; formal vs. informal register; choosing the most precise word.
lessons.key_vocabulary: parallel structure, concision, redundancy, precision, formal style
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students keep redundant phrases like "each and every single one" because they think longer sounds more formal.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a tight, professional message to a coach or employer.

lessons.lesson_title: Unpacking the prompt and planning a text-based essay
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyze an essay prompt and plan a text-based response with a clear thesis.
lessons.key_concepts: Identify the task verb (argue, explain, analyze), the required texts, and the audience; write a thesis that directly answers the prompt; quick outline of 2-3 body points with planned evidence.
lessons.key_vocabulary: prompt, task, thesis, outline, controlling idea
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write an argumentative thesis when the prompt asks them to explain or analyze, or write a general essay that never uses the provided texts.
lessons.real_world_hook: Planning a speech or presentation that actually answers the question you were asked.

lessons.lesson_title: Citing and explaining textual evidence
lessons.learning_objective: I can integrate quotations and paraphrases and explain how they support my claim.
lessons.key_concepts: Introduce evidence with a signal phrase and source; quote briefly and accurately; follow every quotation with explanation (how it proves the point); cite paragraph or line when required.
lessons.key_vocabulary: evidence, signal phrase, paraphrase, quotation, analysis, citation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students drop a quotation into a paragraph and move on without any sentence explaining how it supports the claim.
lessons.real_world_hook: Backing up a recommendation at work with specific data and explaining why it matters.

lessons.lesson_title: Short constructed responses
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a short constructed response that answers the question, cites evidence, and explains it.
lessons.key_concepts: Restate and answer (claim), cite evidence, explain (RACE or similar); answer every part of a multi-part question; stay concise.
lessons.key_vocabulary: constructed response, claim, evidence, explanation, RACE
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students answer only the first part of a two-part question (e.g., identify the theme but never explain how it develops).
lessons.real_world_hook: Answering a customer's question fully and specifically in one short reply.

lessons.lesson_title: Timed writing and self-scoring with a rubric
lessons.learning_objective: I can manage time on an extended response and evaluate my essay against a rubric.
lessons.key_concepts: Budget time to plan, draft, and revise; typical rubric traits (development and organization, evidence and elaboration, conventions); score a sample and your own essay; check your state's own rubric and time limits.
lessons.key_vocabulary: rubric, elaboration, organization, conventions, timed writing, revision
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students spend almost all the time drafting and never reread, leaving missing words and an unfinished conclusion.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a clear report under a deadline at work or in college.

practices.what_students_do: Students read a passage slowly, mark patterns, and reread with a focused question. They annotate diction, syntax, structure, and figurative language.
practices.implications: Each unit includes at least one close-reading lesson; teachers model with a think-aloud.

practices.what_students_do: Students select the strongest evidence, quote or paraphrase accurately, and integrate it with signal phrases.
practices.implications: Evidence quality, not quantity, is graded on every analytic task; rubrics distinguish strong from sufficient.

practices.what_students_do: Students explain how authorial choices about word, sentence, paragraph, and overall structure shape meaning.
practices.implications: Every literary unit ends with an analytic task on craft, not on plot recall.

practices.what_students_do: Students delineate a writer's claim, reasons, and evidence, then judge validity, relevance, and sufficiency.
practices.implications: Argument evaluation appears in literary, informational, and spoken contexts every year.

practices.what_students_do: Students take a position, develop reasons, gather evidence, and address counterclaims fairly.
practices.implications: Every grade writes a sustained argument; later grades add formal style and synthesis.

practices.what_students_do: Students locate sources, judge credibility, take notes, paraphrase, and cite using MLA basics.
practices.implications: Source evaluation is taught explicitly, not assumed; lateral reading is modeled.

practices.what_students_do: Students revise for structure and evidence and edit for syntax and conventions.
practices.implications: Process writing is required for all major pieces; revision is graded separately from drafting.

practices.what_students_do: Students prepare with evidence, build on others' ideas, and probe reasoning.
practices.implications: Socratic seminars and structured discussion appear at every grade; protocols are taught.

practices.what_students_do: Students present claims and findings clearly and listen to evaluate a speaker's logic and rhetoric.
practices.implications: Each year includes at least one formal presentation graded with a rubric.

practices.practice: Using grammar and conventions in context
practices.what_students_do: Students apply grammar choices for clarity and effect, not as isolated drills.
practices.implications: Grammar is taught inside writing units; mini-lessons connect to current drafts.

misconceptions.misconception: Students give a one-word topic (friendship, love) and call it a theme.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Curriculum often introduces theme through topic prompts; students learn to label, not to claim.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the author saying about this topic? Look for the sentence-level theme statement.
misconceptions.remediation: Use a sentence frame: The author suggests that ____. Practice across short texts before novels.

misconceptions.misconception: Students treat the narrator's view as the author's view.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Younger texts often use a first-person narrator who shares author values, so students overgeneralise.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: does the author endorse this narrator, or is there distance? Look for unreliable narration cues.
misconceptions.remediation: Pair an unreliable narrator with a critical essay so students can hear the gap.

misconceptions.misconception: Students write plot summary and label it analysis.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Summary is easier and is often praised in elementary grades.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what does this paragraph claim, and what evidence supports it? Underline claims, separate from retelling.
misconceptions.remediation: Require a verb of analysis (argues, suggests, complicates) in each topic sentence.

misconceptions.misconception: Students write a strong feeling and call it an argument.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Argument and opinion writing are taught together in earlier grades.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the claim, and what reasons could change a thoughtful person's mind?
misconceptions.remediation: Teach the claim-reason-evidence triplet explicitly; ban I think in argument drafts.

misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse tone (author) with mood (reader feeling).
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Both terms get introduced together and use similar adjective lists.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: whose feeling is this, the writer's or mine? Find diction that creates tone.
misconceptions.remediation: Use a two-column chart: tone evidence vs mood evidence on the same passage.

misconceptions.misconception: Students treat dictionary meanings as the whole story.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Vocabulary tests reward denotation; classroom reading often does not surface connotation.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what feelings or associations does this word carry? Compare close synonyms.
misconceptions.remediation: Use synonym ladders (slim, thin, gaunt) and discuss why an author chose one.

misconceptions.misconception: Students predict an outcome and call that foreshadowing.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Prediction is taught as a comprehension strategy and looks similar from the outside.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: where in the text did the author plant this clue? Mark the planted detail.
misconceptions.remediation: Require students to underline the textual clue when they claim foreshadowing.

misconceptions.misconception: Students label any repeated image as a theme.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Motif is sometimes introduced without contrast to theme.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: is this a recurring pattern (motif) or a claim about life (theme)? Both can coexist.
misconceptions.remediation: Use a motif log alongside a theme statement to keep both visible.

misconceptions.misconception: Students label every object as a symbol.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Once symbol is taught, students overapply it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: does the text show this object carrying meaning beyond itself, repeatedly?
misconceptions.remediation: Require three pieces of textual evidence to claim a symbol.

misconceptions.misconception: Students label all credentials ethos and miss tone-based ethos.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Ethos is introduced via Aristotle as credibility, which sounds like resume.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: how does the speaker build trust through tone, fairness, and shared values?
misconceptions.remediation: Compare two speakers with similar credentials but different rhetorical ethos.

misconceptions.misconception: Students label any emotional content pathos without checking purpose.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Pathos is often defined as emotion without nuance.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: how is this emotional appeal meant to move the audience toward the claim?
misconceptions.remediation: Require students to link pathos to a specific claim in the speech.

misconceptions.misconception: Students think a paragraph with numbers automatically has strong logos.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Data-rich texts get called logical even when reasoning is weak.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: are the data relevant to the claim, and does the reasoning hold up?
misconceptions.remediation: Audit a data-heavy paragraph for non sequiturs and unsupported leaps.

misconceptions.misconception: Students name the easiest opposing view and dismiss it.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Curricula sometimes treat counterclaim as a checklist box.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the strongest version of the opposing view, and how would you address it?
misconceptions.remediation: Require steelmanning: have students write the counterclaim before they argue.

misconceptions.topic_area: Plagiarism as copy and paste only
misconceptions.misconception: Students think paraphrase without citation is acceptable.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Plagiarism instruction often focuses on quotation only.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: is this idea or wording mine, and have I cited the source?
misconceptions.remediation: Teach paraphrase quality and citation as one lesson, not two separate ones.

misconceptions.misconception: Students dismiss Wikipedia entirely.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Earlier grades taught it as off-limits; the reasoning was not updated.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what does Wikipedia's footnote chain show about evidence?
misconceptions.remediation: Use Wikipedia as a launchpad; require lateral reading on cited sources.

misconceptions.misconception: Students avoid passive voice everywhere.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Grammar checkers flag it indiscriminately.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: who is the actor, and does it matter? Passive may be correct in science or news.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare lab reports and op-eds for appropriate passive vs active voice.

misconceptions.misconception: Students bury claims in long, tangled sentences.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Academic models include long sentences, which get imitated without control.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: can a reader find the subject and verb? Is each clause earning its place?
misconceptions.remediation: Require subject-verb proximity check on every paragraph.

misconceptions.misconception: Students never use fragments, even when deliberate.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Earlier grades drilled fragment correction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: is this fragment intentional and does it work for the audience?
misconceptions.remediation: Read examples from professional essays that use fragments effectively.

misconceptions.topic_area: Thesis at end of intro only
misconceptions.misconception: Students place the thesis only in the last sentence of the intro.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: A formula was taught as if it were the only structure.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: does the placement serve the argument and the reader?
misconceptions.remediation: Read columns and essays that locate the thesis early, late, or returning.

misconceptions.misconception: Students treat the five-paragraph essay as the highest form.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Test prep practices the form repeatedly.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: does your structure serve your claim, or vice versa?
misconceptions.remediation: Have students restructure a five-paragraph essay into a stronger shape.

misconceptions.misconception: Students assume they cannot understand Shakespeare without a translation.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Some classroom practices use modern paraphrase first.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what can you understand from staging, context, and pattern before glossing?
misconceptions.remediation: Start with a short scene read aloud, then layer in close reading.

misconceptions.misconception: Students assume non-rhyming poems are not real poems.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Earlier exposure favours rhyme-driven verse.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the form, and what does it do?
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a rhyming poem and a free verse poem on the same theme.

misconceptions.misconception: Students reread without a focus.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Close reading was introduced without a stance.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what question are you reading for this time?
misconceptions.remediation: Provide a focus question for each rereading pass.

misconceptions.misconception: Students label any sharpness as irony.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Sarcasm is the most familiar form.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the gap between what is stated and what is meant or known?
misconceptions.remediation: Distinguish verbal, situational, and dramatic irony with current examples.

misconceptions.misconception: Students write arguments in an outraged tone.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Comments sections model heat over clarity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what tone will most likely persuade your audience?
misconceptions.remediation: Have students rewrite a strong argument in a calmer register and compare effect.

misconceptions.misconception: Students rely heavily on a single source.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Earlier research projects required only one or two sources.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: who else is talking about this, and where do they disagree?
misconceptions.remediation: Require triangulation: at least three independent sources for major claims.

misconceptions.misconception: Students dismiss a source as biased without evaluating evidence.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Media literacy slogans simplify bias.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the perspective, and what evidence is offered?
misconceptions.remediation: Compare opinion and reporting from the same outlet on the same story.

glossary.definition: A brief reference to a person, place, event, or text outside the work.
A character or force that opposes the protagonist.
A novel that traces a protagonist's growth from youth to maturity.
The methods an author uses to develop a character (direct or indirect).
The point of highest tension in a plot, after which the action turns.
The struggle between opposing forces in a narrative, internal or external.
A gap between what a character knows and what the audience knows.
A character who undergoes significant internal change.
A long narrative poem on heroic subjects, often involving a journey.
Introductory information about characters, setting, and prior events.
The events after the climax that move toward resolution.
A scene set earlier than the main story line.
A character whose qualities contrast with another to highlight traits.
Hints in earlier text that point toward later events.
A story that contains another story or set of stories inside it.
Narration that blends a character's voice with the narrator's.
An archetype where a protagonist departs, faces trials, and returns transformed.
Deliberate exaggeration for effect.
Language that appeals to the senses to create mental pictures.
Beginning a narrative in the middle of the action.
A gap between what is said or expected and what is meant or occurs.
A direct comparison without like or as.
A recurring image, idea, or pattern in a text.
The voice that tells a story; not always the same as the author.
A figure that joins two opposite terms (deafening silence).
A statement that seems contradictory but reveals a truth.
Giving human qualities to nonhuman things.
The arrangement of events in a narrative.
The vantage point from which a story is told (first, third limited, third omniscient).
The central character whose actions drive the narrative.
The settling of conflicts at the end of a narrative.
Events that build tension after the exposition.
The time, place, and social context of a story.
A comparison using like or as.
A speech in which a character on stage speaks alone to reveal thoughts.
A 14-line poem in iambic pentameter, often with a turn (volta).
A group of lines forming a unit in a poem.
A character who does not undergo significant internal change.
A narrative mode that follows continuous thought.
An object, image, or action that stands for something beyond itself.
A central idea or claim about life that a text develops.
The author's attitude toward subject or audience, conveyed through diction and syntax.
A protagonist of high standing whose flaw or error leads to downfall.
A narrator whose credibility is compromised.
The turn in a sonnet where thought or argument shifts.
Repetition of the same word or phrase at the start of successive clauses.
Juxtaposition of contrasting ideas in balanced phrases.
Omission of conjunctions for compression or speed.
A balanced structure with reversed order (ask not what your country can do for you).
An appeal based on the speaker's credibility and character.
Appeal to the right moment or timely opportunity.
Understatement using a negation of the opposite (not bad).
An appeal based on reason, evidence, and logic.
Substituting a related term for another (the crown for the king).
Using matching grammatical forms for paired or listed items.
An appeal to the audience's emotions or values.
Repeated use of conjunctions for emphasis (and...and...and).
A question asked for effect, not for an answer.
Substituting a part for the whole or whole for part (all hands on deck).
Deliberately presenting something as less significant than it is.
A construction where the subject performs the action.
